Widespread disruptions at the end of the Late Bronze Age led to the abandonment of its palatial structures and the decentralisation of local governance. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Iolcos; Common languages: Mycenaean Greek; Religion: Mycenaean religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Wanax; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1600 BC; Disestablished: c. 1100 BC

name: Menelaion
label: mycenean greece
description: Menelaion was a major Mycenaean palatial settlement established upon the ridge of Therapne overlooking the Eurotas Valley in Laconia. Serving as the primary political and administrative nexus for the region prior to the rise of classical Sparta, the site featured substantial mansions, storage terraces and royal quarters. Destructive fires during the Bronze Age transition prompted the abandonment of the complex as political authority shifted across the valley. \n\n Status: Palatial kingdom; Capital: Menelaion; Common languages: Mycenaean Greek; Religion: Mycenaean religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Wanax; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1600 BC; Disestablished: c. 1100 BC

name: Mycenae
label: mycenean greece
description: Mycenae was the pre-eminent military stronghold and administrative hub of Late Bronze Age mainland Greece, dominating the north-eastern Peloponnese from its hill citadel above the Argive plain. Enclosed by colossal Cyclopean ramparts and entered through the Lion Gate, the kingdom coordinated expansive trade networks extending to Egypt and the Levant. Systemic societal stress and fire destructions around 1100 BC ended its palatial dominance, ushering in the Greek Dark Ages. \n\n Status: Palatial kingdom; Capital: Mycenae; Common languages: Mycenaean Greek; Religion: Mycenaean religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Wanax; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1600 BC; Disestablished: c. 1100 BC

name: Olmecs
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Olmecs established one of the earliest complex civilisations in Mesoamerica, flourishing across the alluvial lowlands of Veracruz and Tabasco. Renowned for monumental basalt portrait heads, ritual earthwork platforms and elaborate jade craftsmanship, their urban centres at San Lorenzo and La Venta coordinated extensive long-distance exchange. Environmental changes and shifting river networks contributed to the gradual abandonment of their principal ceremonial complexes by the fourth century BC. \n\n Status: Civilisation; Capital: San Lorenzo; Common languages: Mixe-Zoquean languages; Religion: Olmec religion; Government: Theocratic chiefdom; Historical era: Mesoamerican Formative period; Established: c. 1600 BC; Disestablished: c. 350 BC

name: Orchomenos
label: mycenean greece
description: Orchomenos was a prosperous Mycenaean kingdom centred in northern Boeotia beside the once-expansive wetlands of Lake Copais. The rulers directed monumental hydraulic engineering works that successfully drained the basin for intensive agriculture, securing immense wealth reflected in their grand tholos tombs. Destructive conflicts with neighbouring Boeotian centres alongside the broader Late Bronze Age collapse brought an end to its palatial hegemony. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Orchomenos; Common languages: Mycenaean Greek; Religion: Mycenaean religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Wanax; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1600 BC; Disestablished: c. 1100 BC

name: Pylos
label: mycenean greece
description: Pylos was a prominent Mycenaean kingdom controlling the fertile coastal lands and natural harbours of Messenia in the south-western Peloponnese. Governed from a multi-storey royal palace at Ano Englianos, the administration maintained extensive Linear B clay tablet archives documenting tax collection, bronze manufacturing and military garrisons. A violent fire destruction around the end of the thirteenth century BC extinguished the palatial polity, leaving its urban site deserted. \n\n Status: Palatial kingdom; Capital: Chora; Common languages: Mycenaean Greek; Religion: Mycenaean religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Wanax; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1600 BC; Disestablished: c. 1100 BC

name: Shang
description: The Shang dynasty was a Bronze Age royal state that unified vast agricultural territories across the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River valley. Based at shifting ceremonial capitals including Yin near modern Anyang, the kings exercised political authority through divination rituals recorded on oracle bones and commanded armies equipped with bronze weaponry. Following centuries of hegemony, the dynasty was overthrown by King Wu of Zhou at the Battle of Muye. \n\n Status: Dynasty; Capital: Anyang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Shang state religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shang; Head of state: King; Historical era: Bronze Age; Established: c. 1600 BC; Disestablished: c. 1046 BC; Succeeded by: Zhou dynasty

name: Thebes
label: mycenean greece
description: Thebes was an influential Mycenaean kingdom in eastern Boeotia, ruled from the fortified citadel of the Cadmea. Overlooking fertile agricultural basins, the city commanded strategic overland crossroads between central Greece and the Peloponnese while maintaining diplomatic contacts with Aegean and Near Eastern kingdoms. Catastrophic fires and external warfare during the collapse of the palatial world destroyed the complex, though community settlements survived around the citadel hill. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Thívai; Common languages: Mycenaean Greek; Religion: Mycenaean religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Wanax; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1600 BC; Disestablished: c. 1100 BC

name: Karduniash
description: Karduniash was the ancient Kassite kingdom established over Babylonia following the collapse of the First Dynasty of Babylon. Governed from the historic metropolis of Babylon and later the fortified citadel of Dur-Kurigalzu, the realm enjoyed internal political stability, thriving international commerce and diplomatic parity with Egypt and the Hittites. Prolonged military conflicts with neighbouring Elam and the Middle Assyrian Empire eventually brought down the dynasty in the twelfth century BC. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Babylon; Common languages: Akkadian and Kassite; Religion: Ancient Mesopotamian religion; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kassite dynasty; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1595 BC; Disestablished: c. 1155 BC; Succeeded by: Second Dynasty of Isin

name: Kingdom of Aleppo
description: The Kingdom of Aleppo was a northern Syrian state centred on the ancient trading metropolis of Yamhad in the fertile valley of the Quweiq River. Following its initial sack by Hittite forces, the territory re-emerged as an autonomous Hurrian-dominated polity that preserved vital transit routes between Anatolia and Mesopotamia. The kingdom continually balanced its autonomy against expanding Hittite and Mitanni ambitions until Suppiluliuma I annexed the territory into a Hittite viceroyalty. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Aleppo; Common languages: Hurrian, Amorite and Akkadian; Religion: Hurrian religion and Ancient Mesopotamian religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Bronze Age; Established: c. 1594 BC; Disestablished: c. 1350 BC; Succeeded by: Hittite Empire

name: Kingdom of Nédjeh
label: second intermediate period of egypt
description: The Kingdom of Nédjeh emerged as a localised political entity during the fragmentation of central authority in the Second Intermediate Period. Linked in administrative records to Upper Egyptian and desert frontier jurisdictions under Seventeenth Dynasty control, the territory safeguarded strategic trade trails and desert outposts. As Theban pharaohs consolidated their authority along the Nile, regional frontier dependencies were progressively reintegrated into the unified administrative hierarchy of the New Kingdom. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Riyadh; Common languages: Egyptian; Religion: Ancient Egyptian religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Seventeenth Dynasty; Historical era: Bronze Age; Established: c. 1570 BC; Disestablished: c. 1560 BC; Succeeded by: Seventeenth Dynasty of Egypt

name: Mitanni
description: Mitanni was a powerful Hurrian-speaking empire centred in the Khabur River basin of northern Syria and south-eastern Anatolia, governed from its royal capital at Washukanni. Renowned for aristocratic chariot warfare and Indo-Aryan cultural elements, the realm exercised hegemony over neighbouring Syrian city-states and northern Mesopotamia. Rising military confrontation with the New Kingdom of Hittites and the newly revived Middle Assyrian Empire steadily eroded its borders until the state was fully dismembered. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Washukanni; Common languages: Hurrian and Akkadian; Religion: Hurrian religion and Ancient Mesopotamian religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1517 BC; Disestablished: c. 1244 BC; Succeeded by: Middle Assyrian Empire

name: Gandhara Kingdom
label: mahajanapadas
description: The Gandhara Kingdom was an ancient realm situated across the Vale of Peshawar and the lower Kabul River basin in north-western South Asia. Renowned in early Vedic literature and counted among the classic sixteen mahajanapadas, the state grew prosperous through fertile alluvial agriculture and its commanding position on trans-continental caravan roads. It maintained grand royal centres at Taxila and Pushkalavati until being incorporated into the Achaemenid Empire under Darius I. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Taxila; Common languages: Gandhari and Sanskrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion, Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1500 BC; Disestablished: c. 535 BC; Succeeded by: Achaemenid Empire

name: Kaminaljuyu
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Kaminaljuyu was a major pre-Columbian ceremonial and political centre located in the fertile Valley of Guatemala within the southern Maya highlands. Beginning as an early agrarian settlement, the polity developed into a sophisticated regional hub featuring extensive earthen mounds, paved plazas and irrigated canal networks. Dominating trade in obsidian and jade throughout the Formative and Classic periods, the city exerted substantial cultural and economic influence across southern Mesoamerica. \n\n Status: City-state; Administrative seat: Kaminaljuyu; Common languages: Maya languages; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Historical era: Pre-Classic to Classic Mesoamerica; Established: c. 1500 BC; Disestablished: c. 401 AD

name: Assuwa League
description: The Assuwa League was an ancient confederation of twenty-two allied states located across north-western Anatolia along the Aegean coast. Formed to resist the aggressive westward expansion of the Hittite Empire, the coalition brought together diverse coastal and inland principalities. Hittite records indicate that Great King Tudhaliya I led a punitive expedition that shattered the allied coalition, taking tens of thousands of prisoners back to central Anatolia. \n\n Status: Confederation; Capital: Assuwa; Common languages: Luwian and related Anatolian languages; Religion: Anatolian polytheism; Government: Military confederation; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1450 BC; Disestablished: c. 1400 BC; Succeeded by: Hittite Empire

name: Assyrian Empire
description: During the middle of the second millennium BC, the Assyrian state centred at Assur fell under the suzerainty of the Hurrian empire of Mitanni. As a subordinate vassal entity, the city paid tribute, surrendered strategic border districts and suffered the removal of royal treasures to Washukanni. This era of foreign subordination ended when King Ashur-uballit I exploited internal Mitannian turmoil to assert full independence and establish the Middle Assyrian Empire. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Assur; Common languages: Akkadian; Religion: Ancient Mesopotamian religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1450 BC; Disestablished: c. 1392 BC; Preceded by: Old Assyrian Empire; Succeeded by: Middle Assyrian Empire

name: Amurru Kingdom
description: The Amurru Kingdom was a strategic Levantine state situated across the Akkar plain and coastal foothills between Byblos and the Orontes River. During the fourteenth century BC, local rulers such as Abdi-Ashirta maintained tributary vassal status under the New Kingdom of Egypt, balancing Nilotic interests against neighbouring regional powers. Royal correspondence preserved in the Amarna Letters documents the kingdom's gradual political pivot toward the expanding Hittite sphere of influence. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Sumur; Common languages: Amorite, Canaanite and Akkadian; Religion: Levantine polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1400 BC; Disestablished: c. 1322 BC; Succeeded by: Hittite Empire

name: Kingdom of Shupria
description: The Kingdom of Shupria was an ancient highland state located north of the upper Tigris River and south-west of Lake Van in the southern Armenian highlands. Inhabited by a diverse population of Hurrians and early regional peoples, the realm acted as a strategic buffer between the rival empires of Assyria and Urartu. Its rulers successfully leveraged rugged mountain fortifications to safeguard their independence and shelter political fugitives from neighbouring imperial domains. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Til-Abni; Common languages: Hurrian and Proto-Armenian; Religion: Ancient Near Eastern polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1400 BC; Disestablished: c. 1300 BC

name: Nakbe
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Nakbe was an early monumental Maya urban centre located in the Mirador Basin within the Peten lowlands of northern Guatemala. Developing into a major regional hub during the Middle Formative period, the city constructed massive terraced limestone platforms, monumental temple pyramids and interconnecting raised causeways. The settlement coordinated long-distance trade in exotic basalt, shell and obsidian until political dominance shifted toward neighbouring El Mirador. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Nakbe; Common languages: Maya languages; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Pre-Classic Maya; Established: c. 1400 BC; Disestablished: c. 201 AD

name: Šeḫa
description: Šeḫa was a prominent Luwian riverland kingdom in western Anatolia, encompassing the fertile valleys of the Bakircay and Gediz rivers in historic Lydia. Set within the cultural orbit of Arzawa, the state frequently shifted alliances between the Hittite Crown and independent Aegean-backed coalitions. Despite occasional rebellions orchestrated with support from Ahhiyawa, Hittite punitive expeditions repeatedly forced its monarchs into negotiated vassalage and tribute treaties. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Sardis; Common languages: Luwian and Hittite; Religion: Anatolian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1400 BC; Disestablished: c. 1300 BC; Succeeded by: Hittite Empire

name: Hayasa-Azzi
description: Hayasa-Azzi was a Late Bronze Age tribal confederation situated in the rugged Armenian Highlands south of the Pontic Alps and Trabzon. Composed of the allied territories of Hayasa and Azzi, the union constituted a formidable northern rival to the Hittite Empire along the upper Euphrates frontier. Repeated Hittite imperial campaigns under Suppiluliuma I and Mursili II sought to neutralise Hayasan raids before the confederacy dissolved during the regional collapse. \n\n Status: Confederation; Capital: Kemah; Common languages: Hurro-Urartian and Proto-Armenian; Religion: Anatolian polytheism; Government: Tribal confederation; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1360 BC; Disestablished: c. 1312 BC; Succeeded by: Nairi

name: Amurru Kingdom
description: During the late fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BC, the Amurru Kingdom operated as a strategic client state under the suzerainty of the Hittite Empire. Administering coastal Syrian ports and the fertile Akkar plain from its capital at Sumur, King Aziru and his successors provided military levies and intelligence to Hattusa. This vassal status positioned Amurru as a primary frontline battleground during imperial confrontations between Hittite and Egyptian armies. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Sumur; Common languages: Amorite and Akkadian; Religion: Levantine polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1322 BC; Disestablished: c. 1275 BC; Preceded by: New Kingdom of Egypt; Succeeded by: Sea Peoples

name: Argethia
label: greek poleis
description: Argethia was an ancient mountain polis and the capital of the Athamanes, situated among the rugged Pindus ranges of south-eastern Epirus and western Thessaly. Perched above defensible highland valleys, the community controlled critical passes connecting western and eastern Greece. Athamanian citizens engaged in pastoral transhumance, maintained local democratic assemblies and fiercely defended their territorial autonomy across centuries of Macedonian and Roman regional conflicts. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Argithea; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek religion; Government: Tribal democracy; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: c. 1300 BC; Disestablished: c. 168 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Bit-Zamani
label: aramean polities
description: Bit-Zamani was a powerful Aramean tribal kingdom situated in northern Mesopotamia within the mountainous Tur Abdin district, governing from the fortified city of Amida on the upper Tigris. Benefiting from productive agricultural terraces and commanding strategic crossroads into the Armenian highlands, the state maintained regional autonomy alongside neighbouring tribal polities. Decades of escalating border warfare against the Neo-Assyrian Empire culminated in its annexation by Ashurnasirpal II. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Amida; Common languages: Aramaic and Akkadian; Religion: Ancient Mesopotamian religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Tur Abdin; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1300 BC; Disestablished: c. 856 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Kingdom of Colchis
description: The Kingdom of Colchis was an ancient Georgian state established along the eastern coast of the Black Sea and the fertile Rioni River basin in western Georgia. Renowned in classical Greek literature as the destination of Jason and the Argonauts, the realm possessed extensive alluvial gold deposits, timber resources and metallurgical traditions. The kingdom cultivated active mercantile connections with Greek colonial poleis before eventually succumbing to the Kingdom of Pontus. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Aea; Common languages: Zan and Ancient Greek; Religion: Georgian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age to Classical antiquity; Established: c. 1300 BC; Disestablished: c. 107 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Pontus

name: Kingdom of Edom
description: The Kingdom of Edom was an ancient Levantine state situated in the mountainous highlands of southern Jordan and the Arabah Valley. Dominating profitable trans-desert trade routes and substantial copper mining operations around Punon, the kingdom maintained a competitive rivalry with neighbouring Judah and Moab. Pressure from nomadic tribes and Babylonian military expeditions under Nabonidus ultimately prompted Edomite communities to migrate westward into southern Judea. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Bozrah; Common languages: Edomite; Religion: Canaanite religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1300 BC; Disestablished: c. 125 BC; Succeeded by: Idumea

name: Kingdom of Moab
description: The Kingdom of Moab was an ancient Levantine state situated upon the mountainous plateau east of the Dead Sea in modern-day central Jordan. Sustained by pastoral agriculture, viticulture and the lucrative King's Highway caravan corridor, the realm frequently clashed with neighbouring Israelite and Ammonite polities. Under King Mesha during the ninth century BC, the kingdom threw off foreign subjugation and expanded its fortified cities before eventually falling to Babylonian hegemony. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Dibon; Common languages: Moabite; Religion: Canaanite religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1300 BC; Disestablished: c. 400 BC; Succeeded by: Nabataean Kingdom

name: Kition
label: cyprus petty kingdoms;phoenician polities (outside phoenicia)
description: Kition was an ancient coastal city-kingdom situated on the southern shore of Cyprus at modern Larnaca. Originally developed during the Late Bronze Age with cyclopean fortifications and copper-processing quarters, the settlement later welcomed Phoenician colonists who established a major naval station and commercial emporium. The city maintained an autonomous royal dynasty through alternating Egyptian and Persian suzerainty until Ptolemy I Soter abolished the kingdom. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Kition; Common languages: Greek and Phoenician; Religion: Ancient Greek religion and Phoenician religion; Government: Monarchy; Currency: Stater; Historical era: Bronze Age to Hellenistic period; Established: c. 1300 BC; Disestablished: c. 312 BC; Succeeded by: Ptolemaic Kingdom

name: Shupria
description: Shupria was an autonomous highland kingdom positioned north of the upper Tigris River, centred near Ubbumu in south-eastern Anatolia. Maintaining a distinct Hurro-Urartian heritage during a period of imperial transition, the polity resisted expanding Middle Assyrian incursions and maintained independence through defensive mountain strongholds. Its location along key trade corridors between Mesopotamia and the Armenian plateau made it an enduring strategic prize for surrounding empires. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Ubbumu; Common languages: Hurrian; Religion: Hurrian religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Late Bronze Age; Established: c. 1300 BC; Disestablished: c. 1275 BC; Succeeded by: Middle Assyrian Empire

name: Pundravardhana Kingdom
description: The Pundravardhana Kingdom was an ancient Iron Age realm situated across northern Bengal and the lower Brahmaputra River basin. Governed from the fortified city of Pundranagara at Mahasthangarh, the state flourished through intensive rice cultivation, riverine trade networks and distinctive metallurgical craftsmanship. The kingdom preserved independent cultural traditions before being drawn into the expanding imperial orbit of northern Indian dynasties, culminating in its incorporation into the Mauryan Empire. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Pundranagara; Common languages: Sanskrit, Prakrit and early Bengali; Religion: Historical Vedic religion, Jainism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1280 BC; Disestablished: c. 280 BC; Succeeded by: Maurya Empire

name: Musri
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Musri was an ancient Syro-Hittite kingdom situated in the foothills and river valleys of the northern Jazira near the upper Tigris basin. Emerging during the decentralisation that followed the collapse of the Hittite Empire, the state united local Luwian and Aramean populations while preserving regional trade corridors. The kingdom fiercely defended its autonomy until sustained military campaigns by Middle and Neo-Assyrian monarchs brought the territory under direct imperial administration. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Musri; Common languages: Luwian, Aramaic and Akkadian; Religion: Anatolian polytheism and Ancient Mesopotamian religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Late Bronze Age to Iron Age; Established: c. 1260 BC; Disestablished: c. 1076 BC; Succeeded by: Middle Assyrian Empire

name: Arados
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (phoenicia)
description: Arados was an influential Phoenician island city-state situated just off the Syrian coast opposite Tartus. Encircled by formidable sea walls, the islanders leveraged their secure offshore redoubt to dominate maritime shipping, ship building and deep-sea fishing throughout the eastern Mediterranean. The city commanded continental trading ports along the adjacent mainland while maintaining local autonomy across changing regional balances of power. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Arwad; Common languages: Phoenician; Religion: Phoenician religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1230 BC; Disestablished: c. 841 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Beirut
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (phoenicia)
description: Beirut was an ancient Phoenician coastal city-state positioned on a rocky promontory along the central Lebanese littoral. Operating as a sheltered anchorage between Byblos and Sidon, the settlement engaged in vibrant regional commerce, timber export and textile manufacturing. While frequently eclipsed politically by larger neighbouring maritime centres, Beirut preserved its hereditary monarchy and civic institutions until imperial Assyrian conquests transformed regional Levantine administration. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Beirut; Common languages: Phoenician; Religion: Phoenician religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1230 BC; Disestablished: c. 856 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Byblos
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (phoenicia)
description: Byblos was an ancient Phoenician maritime city-state situated along the Mount Lebanon coastline north of modern Beirut. Renowned as a primary emporium for cedar timber, papyrus distribution and luxury craft production, the harbour city maintained deep cultural and commercial links across the Mediterranean. Its hereditary kings governed under local civic councils until intensifying Neo-Assyrian military incursions brought the prosperous merchant centre into the imperial tributary network. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Byblos; Common languages: Phoenician; Religion: Phoenician religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1230 BC; Disestablished: c. 841 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Sidon
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (phoenicia)
description: Sidon was a pre-eminent Phoenician port kingdom situated on the southern coast of modern Lebanon. Famed for its specialised production of purple dye, fine glassware and expansive naval expeditions, the city competed directly with Tyre for leadership across Canaanite maritime commerce. Even when subjected to intermittent imperial oversight from Assyria, Babylon and Persia, Sidonian monarchs retained significant internal autonomy and supplied vital fleets for Mediterranean naval operations. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Sidon; Common languages: Phoenician; Religion: Phoenician religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age to Classical antiquity; Established: c. 1230 BC; Disestablished: c. 333 BC; Succeeded by: Macedonian Empire

name: Tyros
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (phoenicia)
description: Tyros was a powerhouse Phoenician city-state established upon a heavily fortified island fortress off the southern coast of Lebanon. Commanding vast fleets across the Mediterranean, Tyrian navigators and merchants established distant colonial foundations including Carthage, Cadiz and Kition while monopolising the maritime trade in purple textiles and metals. Its monarchs successfully rebuffed continental sieges for centuries before being integrated into regional imperial tributary systems. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Tyre; Common languages: Phoenician; Religion: Phoenician religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1230 BC; Disestablished: c. 841 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Argos
label: greek poleis
description: Argos was an ancient Greek polis situated in the fertile Argive plain of the north-eastern Peloponnese. Emerging from the fragmented remnants of the Mycenaean period, the city developed into a powerful Dorian city-state that contested regional supremacy with Sparta. Under the leadership of energetic tyrants such as Pheidon, Argos spearheaded military reforms and established lasting political and religious institutions before eventually joining the Achaean League. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Argos; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek religion; Government: Monarchy, later oligarchy and democracy; Historical era: Iron Age to Hellenistic period; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 229 BC; Succeeded by: Achaean League

name: Bit Bahiani
label: aramean polities
description: Bit Bahiani was an independent Aramean tribal kingdom established in the upper Khabur River basin of north-eastern Syria, centred on the fortified citadel of Guzana at Tell Halaf. The realm flourished through intensive grain cultivation and overland trade, leaving behind remarkable basalt palace reliefs and stone statuary commissioned by King Kapara. The principality maintained its sovereign identity until expanding Neo-Assyrian forces annexed Guzana as an imperial provincial capital. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Guzana; Common languages: Aramaic and Akkadian; Religion: Levantine polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 808 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Bit-Istar
label: bronze age levant city-states
description: Bit-Istar was an ancient highland principality and urban settlement located in the western Zagros Mountains near modern Ravansar in western Iran. Positioned along upland pastoral routes east of the Diyala River, the community developed around a prominent perennial spring and temple precinct dedicated to the goddess Ishtar. The polity preserved local autonomy among Zagros mountain tribes until King Burburazu submitted and rendered tribute during the eastern campaigns of Sargon II. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Bit-Istar; Common languages: Akkadian and early Iranian; Religion: Ancient Mesopotamian religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Zagros Mountains; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 714 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Caria
description: Caria was an ancient south-western Anatolian realm encompassing rugged coastal peninsulas and fertile inland valleys between the Maeander River and Lycia. Governed from internal centres like Mylasa, the indigenous Carian population developed a distinctive Luwian-related tongue and earned fame across the Mediterranean as skilled mercenary soldiers and naval navigators. Regional dynasts preserved territorial independence against Phrygian and Lydian expansion until Cyrus the Great incorporated Caria into the Persian Empire. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Mylasa; Common languages: Carian and Luwian; Religion: Anatolian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Caria; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 556 BC; Succeeded by: Achaemenid Empire

name: Chiapa de Corzo
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Chiapa de Corzo was a major pre-Columbian regional centre located along the Grijalva River in the central depression of Chiapas. Emerging as a prominent Formative period settlement with extensive ceremonial architecture, the city functioned as an essential trading nexus linking the Gulf Coast Olmec cultural sphere with the Pacific littoral. The polity maintained sustained urban occupation and sophisticated ceramic traditions across successive cultural transitions into the Classic period. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Chiapa de Corzo; Common languages: Mixe-Zoquean languages; Religion: Mesoamerican religion; Government: Theocratic chiefdom; Historical era: Mesoamerican Formative to Classic; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 401 AD

name: Diauehi
description: Diauehi was a powerful tribal confederation and early kingdom situated in the rugged highland plateau of north-eastern Anatolia along the upper valleys of the Kura and Coruh rivers. Recorded in royal inscriptions of Tiglath-Pileser I and Shalmaneser III, the realm commanded abundant livestock and sophisticated metallurgical workshops. Despite mounted resistance against Assyrian campaigns, growing military pressure from the expanding southern kingdom of Urartu eventually fractured the confederation. \n\n Status: Confederation; Capital: Zua; Common languages: Proto-Kartvelian, Hurrian and Proto-Armenian; Religion: Ancient Near Eastern polytheism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 750 BC; Succeeded by: Urartu and Colchis

name: El Trapiche
label: mesoamerican polities
description: El Trapiche was an early pre-Columbian ceremonial and political centre located in the Chalchuapa archaeological zone of western El Salvador. Featuring substantial earthen temple mounds, plazas and obsidian workshop complexes, the site participated actively in regional trade networks connecting highland Maya communities with Gulf Coast Olmec spheres. The settlement anchored local agricultural populations and religious observances until volcanic eruptions and shifting regional power dynamics reshaped local settlement patterns. \n\n Status: Ceremonial centre; Capital: El Trapiche; Common languages: Maya languages and Mixe-Zoquean; Religion: Mesoamerican religion; Government: Chiefdom; Historical era: Pre-Classic Mesoamerica; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 201 AD

name: Erythrai
label: greek poleis
description: Erythrai was an ancient Boeotian polis situated along the northern slopes of Mount Cithaeron south of the Asopus River in central Greece. Controlling an upland agrarian territory near the Attic border, the town frequently coordinated local defence alongside its neighbour Hysiai. The community took part in regional military engagements during the Greco-Persian Wars before being gradually overshadowed and administratively subsumed by the expanding federal hegemony of Thebes. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Erythrai; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek religion; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Archaic to Classical Greece; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 446 BC; Succeeded by: Boeotian League

name: Ishtunda
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Ishtunda was an ancient Syro-Hittite kingdom lying across the Cilician plain and Taurus Mountain foothills around the fortified citadel of Karatepe. Arising from the dissolution of imperial Hittite control, the state integrated Luwian and early Danunite populations under hereditary local dynasties. Its rulers erected bilingual inscriptions and elaborate stone gate reliefs while defending their mountain frontiers until Neo-Assyrian imperial armies absorbed the Cilician principalities into provincial administrative units. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Karatepe; Common languages: Luwian and Phoenician; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 900 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Kingdom of Phrygia
description: The Kingdom of Phrygia was an influential Iron Age realm situated across the central Anatolian plateau along the Sangarios River, ruled from the fortified citadel of Gordion. Achieving immense geopolitical prominence under King Midas, the kingdom was celebrated for monumental tumuli burials, intricate bronze metallurgy and stone rock-cut sanctuaries. Devastating nomadic Cimmerian invasions in the early seventh century BC sacked Gordion, ending Phrygian dominance and facilitating subsequent Lydian subjugation. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Gordion; Common languages: Phrygian; Religion: Phrygian religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 675 BC; Succeeded by: Lydia

name: Kuru Kingdom
label: mahajanapadas
description: The Kuru Kingdom was a seminal Vedic state established in northern South Asia across modern Haryana, Delhi and western Uttar Pradesh. As the earliest recorded state-level polity in the Indian subcontinent, Kuru monarchs codified Vedic rituals, standardised ritual sacrifices and arranged sacred hymns into the canonical Vedas. While central royal authority waned during the later Vedic period, Kuru dynastic lineage and traditions formed the historical backdrop for the Mahabharata epic. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Hastinapur; Common languages: Vedic Sanskrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 500 BC; Succeeded by: Vatsa

name: Nairi
description: Nairi was a formidable highland confederation of tribal principalities situated across the rugged plateau between Lake Van, Lake Urmia and the upper Tigris basin. Described in Middle Assyrian royal annals as a loose league of tens of local kings, the Nairi tribes deployed vast herds of horses and infantry to resist imperial incursions. Their coordinated political and military structures formed the direct territorial and cultural foundation for the unified kingdom of Urartu. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: Tushpa; Common languages: Hurro-Urartian; Religion: Ancient Near Eastern polytheism; Government: Confederation; Historical region: Armenian Highlands; Historical era: Late Bronze Age to Iron Age; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 1000 BC; Succeeded by: Urartu

name: Paphlagonia
description: Paphlagonia was an ancient coastal realm and ethnic district situated along the southern Black Sea coast between the Bithynian hills and the Halys River. Celebrated in early literature as a land of skilled horse breeders and sturdy timber shipbuilders, its native communities inhabited inland mountain strongholds and coastal fishing settlements. The Paphlagonians preserved distinct political customs and local dynasts until the territorial expansion of neighbouring Lydia and the Achaemenid Empire curtailed their sovereignty. \n\n Status: Regional polity; Capital: Gangra; Common languages: Palaic and Luwian; Religion: Anatolian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Paphlagonia; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 600 BC; Succeeded by: Lydia

name: Philistine Confederation
description: The Philistine Confederation was an alliance of five fortified city-states, known as the Pentapolis, established along the southern coastal plain of Canaan. Comprising Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gath and Ekron, the confederacy integrated Aegean migrant groups with indigenous Canaanite populations, developing distinctive monochrome pottery and advanced metallurgy. The allied cities maintained commercial and military parity with the kingdoms of Israel and Judah before being devastated and annexed by Neo-Babylonian campaigns under Nebuchadnezzar II. \n\n Status: Confederation; Capital: Gaza; Common languages: Philistine and Canaanite; Religion: Canaanite religion; Government: Oligarchical confederation; Ruler title: Seren; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 604 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Babylonian Empire

name: Ujuxte
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Ujuxte was a sprawling pre-Columbian urban centre situated on the Pacific coastal plain of western Guatemala within the Retalhuleu Department. Constructed with a formal gridded layout aligned to astronomical axes, the city featured massive earthen temple mounds, wide plazas and raised residential platforms. Dominating fertile agricultural lands and regional trade corridors in cacao, salt and obsidian, Ujuxte served as a major regional power before collapsing during the Late Preclassic period. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Ujuxte; Common languages: Mixe-Zoquean and early Maya; Religion: Mesoamerican religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Pre-Classic Mesoamerica; Established: c. 1200 BC; Disestablished: c. 201 AD

name: Domain of Amenmesse
description: The Domain of Amenmesse was a short-lived breakaway realm centred on Thebes during the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt. Seizing control of Upper Egypt and Kush from the legitimate heir Seti II, Amenmesse claimed pharaonic titles and governed southern administrative centres for several years. His rival administration controlled Nubian gold revenues and temple estates until Seti II re-established royal authority throughout the Nile Valley and erased his predecessor's monuments. \n\n Status: Secessionist realm; Capital: Thebes; Common languages: Egyptian; Religion: Ancient Egyptian religion; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nineteenth Dynasty; Ruler title: Pharaoh; Historical era: Bronze Age; Established: c. 1197 BC; Disestablished: c. 1195 BC; Succeeded by: New Kingdom of Egypt

name: Bit-Adini
label: aramean polities
description: Bit-Adini was a major Aramean tribal kingdom established along both banks of the middle Euphrates River south of Carchemish, governed from the fortified stronghold of Til Barsip. Controlling critical river crossings and trade routes linking Mesopotamia with northern Syria, the realm commanded considerable wealth and fielded formidable armies. Assyrian king Shalmaneser III conducted repeated campaigns against King Ahuni, ultimately capturing Til Barsip and absorbing Bit-Adini directly into the Assyrian provincial system. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Til Barsip; Common languages: Aramaic and Luwian; Religion: Levantine polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1180 BC; Disestablished: c. 855 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Hamath
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Hamath was an influential Syro-Hittite kingdom situated in west-central Syria along the fertile valley of the Orontes River. Arising in the wake of imperial Hittite collapse, the state accommodated both Luwian and Aramean cultural communities while establishing extensive irrigation norias to support regional agriculture. Hamath spearheaded regional military coalitions against westward Assyrian expansion until Sargon II captured the city in 720 BC, deporting its inhabitants and turning the territory into an Assyrian province. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Hama; Common languages: Luwian and Aramaic; Religion: Levantine polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1180 BC; Disestablished: c. 720 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Kammanu
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Kammanu was an Iron Age Syro-Hittite kingdom situated on the Malatya Plain north of the Taurus Mountains and west of the upper Euphrates. Inheriting administrative traditions from the collapsed Hittite state, the kingdom flourished through extensive copper working, horse breeding and trade with Anatolian highlands. Its kings resisted external encroachment through shifting alliances with Urartu until the Neo-Assyrian monarch Sargon II conquered the royal citadel of Melid and dismantled the monarchy. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Melid; Common languages: Hieroglyphic Luwian; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1180 BC; Disestablished: c. 712 BC; Preceded by: Hittite Empire; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Kingdom of Sam'al
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: The Kingdom of Sam'al was an ancient Syro-Hittite and Aramean state centred on the heavily fortified citadel of Zincirli in the Anti-Taurus Mountains. Flanked by critical mountain passes linking Cilicia with the northern Syrian plains, the realm was adorned with distinctive bilingual Luwian and Old Aramaic orthostats and monumental palace gates. The kingdom maintained internal autonomy as an Assyrian tributary before being converted into a directly administered imperial province. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Zincirli; Common languages: Samalian, Old Aramaic and Luwian; Religion: Levantine polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1180 BC; Disestablished: c. 740 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Babylon
description: Following the collapse of Kassite rule and brief Elamite raids, Babylon re-emerged as an independent sovereign realm under native Mesopotamian dynasties, notably the Second Dynasty of Isin. Under King Nebuchadnezzar I, the state restored national pride by defeating Elam and recovering the sacred statue of Marduk to the Esagila temple. Babylon navigated intense regional competition and Aramean incursions until intensifying internal rivalries led to growing subjugation under the Neo-Assyrian Empire. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Babylon; Common languages: Akkadian; Religion: Ancient Mesopotamian religion; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Second Dynasty of Isin; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1155 BC; Disestablished: c. 824 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Kourion
label: cyprus petty kingdoms
description: Kourion was an ancient Greek city-kingdom situated atop a high limestone promontory along the south-western coast of Cyprus overlooking Episkopi Bay. Settled by Argive colonists following the collapse of Mycenaean palatial centres, the kingdom thrived on fertile coastal farming, maritime commerce and a famous sanctuary dedicated to Apollo Hylates. The city-state preserved its autonomous royal dynasty through centuries of regional political flux until participating in wider anti-Persian alliances during the Classical era. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Kourion; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age to Classical antiquity; Established: c. 1155 BC; Disestablished: c. 570 BC; Succeeded by: Achaemenid Empire

name: Anarta Kingdom
description: The Anarta Kingdom was an ancient realm situated across the peninsula of Saurashtra and the plains of northern Gujarat in western South Asia. Prominently featured in epic literature including the Mahabharata and Bhagavata Purana, the polity maintained maritime trading connections from harbour settlements including Dvaraka. The state was administered by Yadava lineages who leveraged coastal navigation and fertile pastures before the region assimilated into broader Iron Age janapada structures. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Dvaraka; Common languages: Vedic Sanskrit and early Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Gujarat; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 500 BC; Succeeded by: Saurashtra Kingdom

name: Asmaka Kingdom
label: mahajanapadas
description: The Asmaka Kingdom was an ancient realm situated along the banks of the Godavari River in south-central India, centred on the capital city of Potali at modern Bodhan. Recognised in Buddhist texts as the sole southern mahajanapada among the traditional sixteen great realms, the state occupied an essential commercial conduit linking northern India with the Deccan plateau. The kingdom maintained its independence until its territories were conquered and absorbed into the expanding Magadhan Empire. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Bodhan; Common languages: Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 345 BC; Succeeded by: Nanda Empire

name: Dasarna Kingdom
description: The Dasarna Kingdom was an ancient realm situated in central India along the river valleys of northern Madhya Pradesh south of the Chedi country. Governed by Yadava and Chandravanshi dynastic branches from their fortified seat at Vidisha, the state engaged in regional diplomacy and marital alliances with neighbouring Panchala and Avanti. Its prosperous agrarian heartland and river crossings made Dasarna an active participant in early north Indian trade networks before its eventual political consolidation. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Vidisha; Common languages: Sanskrit and early Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Malwa; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 1000 BC; Succeeded by: Avanti

name: Himalaya Kingdom
description: The Himalaya Kingdom was an ancient mountainous polity situated across the sub-Himalayan valleys and foothills near the upper Ganges River. Governed from historic transit sanctuaries including Haridwar, the kingdom was famed in Puranic accounts as the realm of Himavat, linking lowland agricultural communities with upland mountain tribes. The polity served as a cultural boundary zone and pilgrim crossroads before gradually integrating into the smaller territorial janapadas of northern India. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Haridwar; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Garhwal and Kumaon; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 1000 BC; Succeeded by: Kuninda Kingdom

name: Kasmira Kingdom
description: The Kasmira Kingdom was an ancient realm established within the secluded and fertile Kashmir Valley along the upper Jhelum River in north-western South Asia. Sheltered by surrounding Pir Panjal and Himalayan ranges, the state developed from early Naga and Vedic cultural roots into a thriving agrarian and scholarly centre. Its rulers maintained defensive mountain frontiers and cultivated independent diplomatic contacts across the western Himalayas until regional conquest brought the valley under Mauryan administration. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Srinagar; Common languages: Sanskrit and early Dardic; Religion: Historical Vedic religion and Shaivism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 326 BC; Succeeded by: Maurya Empire

name: Kekeya Kingdom
description: The Kekeya Kingdom was an ancient realm situated in western Punjab between the Jhelum and Chenab rivers in modern Pakistan. Governed by martial kshatriya dynasties celebrated in the Ramayana and Mahabharata epics, the state possessed renowned horse breeding establishments and guarded western frontier trade approaches into the Indo-Gangetic plain. Kekeya princes maintained strategic diplomatic ties with Kosala and neighbouring Gandhara until the territory gradually merged into broader regional janapada leagues. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Kekeya; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical region: Punjab; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 1000 BC; Succeeded by: Madra Kingdom

name: Kingdom of Avanti
label: mahajanapadas
description: The Kingdom of Avanti was a powerful ancient state situated across the Malwa plateau of central India, counted among the classical sixteen mahajanapadas. Bisected by the Vetravati River, the realm was administered from primary urban capitals at Ujjayini and Mahishmati along the vital Dakshinapatha southern trade artery. Avanti developed into an important centre of early Buddhism and metallurgical production before its monarch Nandivardhana was defeated, leading to annexation by the expanding Magadha Empire. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Ujjain; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion, Jainism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 300 BC; Succeeded by: Magadha

name: Kirata Kingdom
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: The Kirata Kingdom was an ancient mountain realm situated across the eastern Himalayan ranges and central hill valleys of modern Nepal. Governed by indigenous Kirata dynasties, the polity drew strength from hardy upland pastoralism, mountain horticulture and strategic command of trans-Himalayan trade trails into Tibet. The kingdom preserved unique animistic and cultural traditions for centuries before the migration of Indo-Aryan clans contributed to the gradual rise of the Licchavi dynasty in the Kathmandu Valley. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Kathmandu; Common languages: Kiranti languages and early Sino-Tibetan; Religion: Kiratism and animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Hang; Historical era: Iron Age to Classical antiquity; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 301 AD; Succeeded by: Licchavi Kingdom

name: Kosala Kingdom
label: mahajanapadas
description: The Kosala Kingdom was a prominent ancient realm situated across the fertile alluvial plains of central Awadh in northern India, north of the Ganges River. Governed from renowned royal cities at Ayodhya and Shravasti, the state emerged as one of the pre-eminent sixteen mahajanapadas and a vibrant cradle for early Buddhist and Jain teachings. Prolonged territorial rivalries with neighbouring Magadha culminated in its eventual military subjugation under King Ajatashatru. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Ayodhya; Common languages: Sanskrit and Kosali Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion, Buddhism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 450 BC; Succeeded by: Magadha

name: Lanka
description: Lanka was an ancient insular kingdom described in South Asian epic traditions as a fortified royal redoubt situated on the island of Sri Lanka. Governed from the mountainous stronghold of Lankapura, the polity was portrayed as controlling abundant tropical maritime wealth, gem mining and elephant herds in the Indian Ocean. The island's early dynastic traditions formed the mythic and cultural precursor for the subsequent historical kingdoms established by Indo-Aryan settlers and indigenous lineages. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Lankapura; Common languages: Early Indo-Aryan and proto-Dravidian; Religion: Ancient Indian religions; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Sri Lanka; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 1000 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Tambapanni

name: Madra Kingdom
description: The Madra Kingdom was an ancient Vedic realm situated in the central Punjab between the Ravi and Chenab rivers, centred on the fortified metropolis of Sagala at modern Sialkot. Renowned for horse breeding, martial chivalry and prominent dynastic marriages with the royal house of Kuru, the polity occupied an essential commercial gateway across north-western South Asia. Madra maintained its territorial integrity until regional political transformations integrated its lands into larger Pan-Indian imperial federations. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Sagala; Common languages: Vedic Sanskrit and early Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical region: Punjab; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 500 BC; Succeeded by: Achaemenid Empire

name: Magadha Kingdom
label: mahajanapadas
description: The Magadha Kingdom was an ancient Indian realm based in southern Bihar south of the Ganges, which developed into the dominant imperial power of ancient South Asia. Administered initially from the hill citadel of Rajagriha and later from the river metropolis of Pataliputra, Magadha prospered through rich iron ore deposits, fertile agriculture and disciplined standing armies. Under the Haryanka, Shaishunaga and Nanda dynasties, the kingdom systematically conquered neighbouring mahajanapadas to establish vast imperial rule. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Rajagriha; Common languages: Sanskrit and Magadhi Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion, Buddhism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 322 BC; Succeeded by: Maurya Empire

name: Nepa Kingdom
description: The Nepa Kingdom was an ancient Himalayan mountain polity situated among the central river basins and southern slopes of the high Himalayas. Described in early Sanskrit literature as an autonomous mountain state, the kingdom maintained strategic passways between the Gangetic plain and the Tibetan plateau. Its inhabitants combined terrace agriculture with transhumant pastoralism, preserving regional independence until broader dynastic consolidations in the Kathmandu Valley formed the foundational basis of early Nepalese kingdoms. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Janakpur; Common languages: Sanskrit and early Tibeto-Burman; Religion: Historical Vedic religion and animism; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Himalayas; Historical era: Iron Age to Antiquity; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 351 AD; Succeeded by: Licchavi Kingdom

name: Pragjyotisha Kingdom
description: The Pragjyotisha Kingdom was an ancient eastern realm situated along the fertile floodplains of the Brahmaputra River in modern Assam. Governed from the citadel of Pragjyotishpura at Guwahati, the kingdom gained prominence in Hindu epic traditions for elephant domestication, advanced astronomy and skilled river navigation. Later rulers of Kamarupa traced their lineage back to legendary Pragjyotisha monarchs to legitimise their authority, cementing the state's cultural foundation in north-eastern India. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Guwahati; Common languages: Early Assamese and Sanskrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion and indigenous animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical region: Kamarupa; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 1000 BC; Succeeded by: Kamarupa

name: Sindhu Kingdom
description: The Sindhu Kingdom was an ancient realm situated along the lower basin of the Indus River in modern Sindh and southern Punjab. Governed from the fortified river capital of Alor, the state drew tremendous economic prosperity from irrigated floodplains, riverine commerce and maritime access to the Arabian Sea. Frequently allied or contested with neighbouring Sauvira, the kingdom defended its western frontier until Persian and subsequent Macedonian campaigns incorporated the lower Indus valley. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Alor; Common languages: Sanskrit and early Sindhi Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical region: Sindh; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 317 BC; Succeeded by: Maurya Empire

name: Suhma Kingdom
description: The Suhma Kingdom was an ancient Late Vedic realm situated in south-western Bengal along the lower reaches of the Hooghly River. Its primary urban and maritime hub at Tamralipta flourished as a major deep-water international port, exporting textiles, silk, grain and copper throughout the Bay of Bengal. Suhma maintained an autonomous political and mercantile identity alongside its eastern neighbours before being systematically absorbed into the expanding sphere of the Magadha Empire. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Tamluk; Common languages: Sanskrit and early Bengali Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion and early Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Bengal; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 1000 BC; Succeeded by: Magadha

name: Trigarta Kingdom
description: The Trigarta Kingdom was an ancient Indo-Aryan realm situated in the northern Punjab plains between the Ravi and Sutlej rivers, extending north into the Kangra Valley. Governed from royal citadels at Prasthala and Jalandhar, the state drew military strength from its warrior guilds and fertile alluvial soils. The kingdom fiercely defended its riverine territories against neighbouring Kuru and Salva federations until Macedonian expeditions and Mauryan unification transformed northern South Asia. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Jalandhar; Common languages: Sanskrit and early Punjabi Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical region: Punjab; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 317 BC; Succeeded by: Maurya Empire

name: Vanga Kingdom
description: The Vanga Kingdom was an ancient maritime realm situated across the deltaic waterways of the lower Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers in southern and eastern Bengal. Famous for its formidable war fleets, maritime shipbuilders and trained battle elephants, the kingdom conducted extensive sea trade linking eastern India with Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia. It maintained an autonomous political identity from major regional emporia like Chandraketugarh until being incorporated into the Nanda Empire. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Chandraketugarh; Common languages: Early Bengali Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion, Jainism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical region: Bengal; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 345 BC; Succeeded by: Nanda Empire

name: Vidarbha Kingdom
description: The Vidarbha Kingdom was an ancient realm situated across the northern Deccan plateau in the fertile valleys of the Wardha and Wainganga rivers in central India. Administered by Yadava dynastic lineages from royal capitals at Kundinapuri and Bhojakata, the state was celebrated in Sanskrit epic traditions for its agricultural prosperity, cotton production and diplomatic alliances. The kingdom maintained sovereign autonomy across the early Iron Age before gradually integrating into subsequent central Indian imperial realms. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Kundinapuri; Common languages: Sanskrit and Maharashtri Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical region: Deccan; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1150 BC; Disestablished: c. 550 BC

name: Palistin
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Palistin was an early Syro-Hittite kingdom situated in the fertile Amuq Valley and the Orontes River delta across north-western Syria and modern Hatay. Governing from the heavily fortified capital of Kunulua at Tell Tayinat, King Taita and his successors united Luwian and Aegean-influenced populations following the fall of the Hittite Empire. The kingdom maintained extensive temple complexes and monumental stone relief art before splintering into smaller successor principalities like Pattin. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Kunulua; Common languages: Luwian; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1109 BC; Disestablished: c. 1000 BC; Preceded by: Hittite Empire; Succeeded by: Pattin

name: Gadir
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (outside phoenicia)
description: Gadir was an ancient Phoenician coastal colony and merchant city-state founded on a narrow barrier island off the Atlantic coast of south-western Iberia. Functioning as the primary maritime gateway for maritime exploration into the Atlantic, the settlement grew immensely wealthy through the export of silver from Tartessos, marine salted fish and purple dye. Governed by a civic magistrate assembly and temple priesthood dedicated to Melqart, Gadir maintained commercial independence until entering the Carthaginian sphere. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Cadiz; Common languages: Phoenician; Religion: Phoenician religion; Government: Oligarchical republic; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1104 BC; Disestablished: c. 530 BC; Succeeded by: Carthaginian Empire

name: Anga Kingdom
label: mahajanapadas
description: The Anga Kingdom was an ancient realm situated in the eastern Gangetic plain east of Magadha, across modern eastern Bihar and adjacent Bengal. Governed from the fortified riverine capital of Champapuri near modern Bhagalpur, the kingdom flourished as a vital hub for overland caravans and maritime merchant voyages descending the Ganges. Anga preserved its sovereign royal house and distinctive cultural identity until King Bimbisara of Magadha conquered the realm in the sixth century BC. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Champapuri; Common languages: Sanskrit and early Magadhi Prakrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion, Jainism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1100 BC; Disestablished: c. 500 BC; Succeeded by: Magadha

name: Aram-Damascus
label: aramean polities
description: Aram-Damascus was a powerful Aramean kingdom established in the fertile Ghouta oasis of the southern Levant, centred on the ancient walled metropolis of Damascus. Commanding key desert caravan trails connecting Mesopotamia, Phoenicia and Arabia, the realm emerged as the chief regional rival to the Kingdom of Israel and the expanding Neo-Assyrian Empire. Under energetic monarchs like Hazael, the state dominated southern Syrian politics until Tiglath-Pileser III captured Damascus in 732 BC. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Damascus; Common languages: Old Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1100 BC; Disestablished: c. 732 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Dahae Confederation
description: The Dahae Confederation was a nomadic alliance of Eastern Iranian pastoral tribes inhabiting the arid steppes and desert margins east of the Caspian Sea and north of the Kopet Dag. Renowned for horse archery, seasonal pastoral mobility and camel breeding, the confederate clans maintained loose political cohesion across the Karakum Desert. The alliance contested frontier borders with neighbouring sedentary oases before its constituent Parni tribe later migrated south to establish the Parthian Empire. \n\n Status: Nomadic confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Eastern Iranian languages; Religion: Scythian religion and Iranian polytheism; Government: Tribal confederation; Historical region: Central Asian Steppe; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1100 BC; Disestablished: c. 1000 BC; Succeeded by: Parni

name: Hippo Diarrhytus
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (outside phoenicia)
description: Hippo Diarrhytus was an ancient Phoenician maritime colony and trading post established at modern Bizerte on the northernmost coastline of Tunisia. Positioned along a natural coastal channel connecting a large interior freshwater lake to the Mediterranean Sea, the settlement provided exceptionally sheltered anchorage for merchant fleets. Operating as an autonomous maritime emporium throughout the early Iron Age, the city-state eventually integrated into the expanding commercial and defensive network of Carthage. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Hippo Diarrhytus; Common languages: Phoenician; Religion: Phoenician religion; Government: Oligarchical republic; Historical region: North Africa; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1100 BC; Disestablished: c. 600 BC; Succeeded by: Carthaginian Empire

name: Marion
label: cyprus petty kingdoms
description: Marion was an ancient Greek city-kingdom situated on the north-western coast of Cyprus in the fertile Akamas region near modern Polis Chrysochous. Blessed with nearby copper deposits in the Troodos foothills and dense timber forests, the city grew wealthy through metallurgical export and maritime commerce across the eastern Mediterranean. Governed by hereditary kings who maintained close cultural ties with Athens, the kingdom preserved its political autonomy until being captured and dismantled by Ptolemy I Soter. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Marion; Common languages: Ancient Greek and Eteocypriot; Religion: Ancient Greek religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age to Hellenistic period; Established: c. 1100 BC; Disestablished: c. 312 BC; Succeeded by: Ptolemaic Kingdom

name: Sirqu
label: aramean polities
description: Sirqu was an ancient Aramean principality and fortified river town situated along the middle Euphrates River at modern Tell Ashara in eastern Syria. Occupying the historic urban site of Terqa, the settlement maintained strategic control over river crossings and caravan trade corridors connecting northern Syria with central Mesopotamia. The local rulers preserved regional political autonomy until aggressive military expansion by Neo-Assyrian kings brought Sirqu under direct imperial provincial governance. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Sirqu; Common languages: Aramaic and Akkadian; Religion: Ancient Mesopotamian religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical region: Middle Euphrates; Historical era: Iron Age; Established: c. 1100 BC; Disestablished: c. 878 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Kingdom of Kush
description: The Kingdom of Kush was an ancient Nubian power centred along the middle Nile Valley in modern Sudan, established around the sacred mountain of Jebel Barkal and the royal seat of Napata. Following the withdrawal of New Kingdom Egyptian administration, Kushite monarchs revived imperial pharaonic traditions, unified the Nile Valley and ruled Egypt as the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty. After retreating south to Meroe, the kingdom flourished through iron smelting, agriculture and extensive Red Sea commerce. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Napata, later Meroë; Common languages: Meroitic and Egyptian; Religion: Ancient Egyptian and Nubian religions; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age to Antiquity; Established: c. 1070 BC; Disestablished: c. 350 AD; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Aksum

name: Bubastis
label: third intermediate period of egypt
description: Bubastis was an ancient Lower Egyptian city-kingdom located in the eastern Nile Delta at modern Tell Basta, renowned as the religious cult centre of the feline goddess Bastet. Emerging as an autonomous power centre amid the political decentralisation of the Third Intermediate Period, the city served as the ancestral home of the Libyan Twenty-Second Dynasty founded by Shoshenq I. Bubastis flourished through pilgrimage traffic, Delta grain revenues and active trade links with the Levant. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Bubastis; Common languages: Egyptian; Religion: Ancient Egyptian religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Twenty-Second Dynasty; Ruler title: Pharaoh; Historical era: Third Intermediate Period; Established: c. 1069 BC; Disestablished: c. 713 BC; Succeeded by: Twenty-Fifth Dynasty of Egypt

name: State of Guan
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Guan was a short-lived Chinese appanage established in central Henan around modern Zhengzhou at the founding of the Western Zhou dynasty. Granted to Shu Xian of Guan, a younger brother of King Wu of Zhou, the territory served as one of the Three Guards tasked with monitoring the defeated Shang heartland. After King Wu died, Guan rebelled alongside the other guards against the Duke of Zhou and was swiftly extinguished following their military defeat. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Guancheng; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion and ancestor veneration; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Western Zhou; Established: c. 1046 BC; Disestablished: c. 1039 BC; Succeeded by: Western Zhou

name: State of Shu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Shu was an ancient independent kingdom situated across the fertile Chengdu Plain in the western Sichuan Basin. Possessing a distinctive metallurgical and artistic tradition exemplified by the bronze artefacts of Sanxingdui and Jinsha, Shu developed in relative isolation behind rugged mountain barriers. The kingdom engaged in periodic warfare and commerce with its eastern neighbour Ba until King Huiwen of Qin dispatched armies that annexed the realm in 316 BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Chengdu; Common languages: Ancient Shu and Old Chinese; Religion: Ancient Sichuanese religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Spring and Autumn to Warring States; Established: c. 1046 BC; Disestablished: c. 316 BC; Succeeded by: State of Qin

name: State of Tan
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Tan was a minor Chinese viscounty established in central Shandong around modern Zhangqiu at the inception of the Western Zhou period. Descended from ancient Dongyi lineages that pledged nominal allegiance to the Zhou court, the state preserved peaceful agricultural communities along the alluvial plains. Due to diplomatic friction and a failure to show proper ritual deference to Duke Huan of Qi, Tan was invaded and annexed by Qi in 684 BC. \n\n Status: Viscounty; Capital: Mingshui; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Viscount; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Established: c. 1046 BC; Disestablished: 684 BC; Succeeded by: State of Qi

name: Zhou
description: The Zhou dynasty was a foundational Chinese royal state that overthrew the Shang dynasty at the Battle of Muye, inaugurating the longest-reigning imperial lineage in Chinese history. Administered from dual western capitals at Haojing and eastern Luoyi, the kings established the Mandate of Heaven doctrine and instituted a decentralised feudal network of allied fiefdoms. While central royal power eroded during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, Zhou ritual prestige endured until its extinction by Qin. \n\n Status: Royal dynasty; Capital: Haojing and Luoyi; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship and Heaven worship; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Bronze Age to Iron Age; Established: c. 1046 BC; Disestablished: 256 BC; Succeeded by: Qin dynasty

name: State of Deng
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Deng was an ancient Chinese marquessate located in the borderlands between southern Henan and northern Hubei, centred near Dengzhou. Ruled by the noble Man clan, the state occupied an essential overland transit corridor connecting the central Yellow River plains with the middle Yangtze valley. Deng maintained close marital and political connections with the southern powerhouse of Chu until Chu forces systematically overwhelmed and annexed the marquessate in 678 BC. \n\n Status: Marquessate; Capital: Dengzhou; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor veneration and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1045 BC; Disestablished: 678 BC; Succeeded by: State of Chu

name: State of E
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of E was an ancient Chinese realm that originated in southern Henan before relocating to Ezhou in modern Hubei along the Yangtze River. Tracing its aristocratic pedigree back to the Shang dynasty, the state commanded lucrative bronze resources and strategic river navigation. Following a massive rebellion against the authority of King Li of Zhou, royal armies crushed the state, though its historical name endured as the lasting regional abbreviation for Hubei. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Ezhou; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion and ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Western Zhou; Established: c. 1045 BC; Disestablished: 863 BC; Succeeded by: State of Chu

name: State of Ge
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Ge was an ancient Chinese feudal polity situated in eastern Henan near modern Ningling, with roots extending back to the Xia and Shang eras. Reconfirmed as a regional barony under the Western Zhou settlement, the state preserved traditional ancestral shrines and modest agrarian territories on the North China Plain. Ge maintained quiet local autonomy alongside larger neighbouring powers until expanding military conflicts during the Spring and Autumn period brought about its absorption. \n\n Status: Barony; Capital: Ge; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Baron; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1045 BC; Disestablished: c. 476 BC; Succeeded by: State of Song

name: State of Guang
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Guang was a minor Chinese feudal principality founded by descendants of the Ji clan, located around modern Guangshan in southern Henan. Occupying an exposed agrarian corridor between the Huai River basin and the Dabie Mountains, the polity frequently balanced between rival regional neighbours. In the mid-seventh century BC, military expansion by the neighbouring State of Huang led directly to the conquest and annexation of Guang. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Guangshan; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion and ancestor worship; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Ruler; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1045 BC; Disestablished: c. 650 BC; Succeeded by: State of Huang

name: State of Lai
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Lai was an ancient Dongyi principality situated on the eastern Shandong Peninsula, governing coastal and mountainous territories around modern Laiwu and Changle. Maintaining distinct cultural and linguistic customs separate from the Zhou court, the state commanded substantial marine resources, salt production and mineral wealth. Lai resisted cultural assimilation and military encroachment by the neighbouring State of Qi for centuries before Duke Ling of Qi conquered and annexed the realm in 567 BC. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Changle; Common languages: Old Chinese and Dongyi languages; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1045 BC; Disestablished: 567 BC; Succeeded by: State of Qi

name: State of Pi
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Pi was an ancient Chinese vassal state located in northern Jiangsu and southern Shandong, centred on modern Pizhou and Xue. Governed by the aristocratic Ren family, the state maintained productive agricultural lands and textile workshops bordered by Song to the west and Tan to the north.
