Pi navigated complex regional alliances throughout the Spring and Autumn period until the aggressive northern expansion of Chu extinguished its independence. \n\n Status: Earldom; Capital: Pizhou; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Earl; Historical era: Western Zhou to Warring States; Established: c. 1045 BC; Disestablished: 418 BC; Succeeded by: State of Chu

name: State of Qi
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Qi was a minor Chinese feudal state situated in eastern Henan near modern Kaifeng, founded by the Zhou court to maintain ancestral sacrifices for the defeated Xia dynasty. Governed by rulers bearing the noble Si surname, the small polity suffered repeated territorial pressures from powerful neighbours and relocated its capital multiple times. Despite its venerable royal lineage, Qi was eventually conquered and disestablished by the expanding armies of Chu in 445 BC. \n\n Status: Feudal state; Capital: Qixian; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Western Zhou to Warring States; Established: c. 1045 BC; Disestablished: 445 BC; Succeeded by: State of Chu

name: State of Sui
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Sui, also identified in modern archaeological scholarship as the State of Zeng, was an influential Chinese polity situated in northern Hubei around Suizhou. Positioned along a critical military corridor defending the Zhou heartland against southern expansion, the state grew wealthy by controlling rich copper trade routes along the Yangtze. The state developed advanced bronze metallurgical casting, exemplified by the famous chime bells of Marquis Yi, before Chu ultimately absorbed the territory. \n\n Status: Marquessate; Capital: Suizhou; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion and ancestor worship; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Western Zhou to Warring States; Established: c. 1045 BC; Disestablished: c. 681 BC; Succeeded by: State of Chu

name: State of Xu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Xu was an ancient Huaiyi realm situated across the fertile Huai River valley in northern Jiangsu and Anhui. Led by the Ying clan, Xu formed a formidable confederation of thirty-six allied states that openly challenged Western Zhou royal armies on the Central Plain. Although forced into periodic vassalage, the kingdom retained remarkable political and cultural independence until prolonged military pressure from Chu and Wu resulted in its final conquest in 512 BC. \n\n Status: Monarchy; Capital: Xu; Common languages: Old Chinese and Huaiyi dialects; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1045 BC; Disestablished: 512 BC; Succeeded by: State of Wu

name: State of Zeng
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Zeng was an ancient Chinese feudal realm located in south-western Henan near modern Fangcheng. Established during the Western Zhou dynasty to anchor royal influence across the northern approaches to the Nanyang Basin, the polity managed local agricultural communities and transit routes. Squeezed between the expanding territorial ambitions of northern principalities and the rising power of Chu, the state was eventually invaded, dismantled and integrated into Chu territory in 567 BC. \n\n Status: Viscounty; Capital: Fangcheng; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Viscount; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1045 BC; Disestablished: 567 BC; Succeeded by: State of Chu

name: State of Ba
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Ba was an ancient confederation of tribal clans established in eastern Sichuan, Chongqing and western Hubei. Inhabiting mountainous river corridors along the upper Yangtze, the Ba people were renowned as fierce warriors, skilled river navigators and suppliers of valuable salt, cinnabar and timber. Although frequently allying with Zhou and Chu against common foes, internal clan divisions left the state vulnerable to King Huiwen of Qin, who annexed Ba in 316 BC. \n\n Status: Confederation; Capital: Chongqing; Common languages: Ancient Ba and Old Chinese; Religion: Ba folk religion and animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Western Zhou to Warring States; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 316 BC; Succeeded by: State of Qin

name: State of Cai
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Cai was an ancient Chinese march established in south-eastern Henan along the upper reaches of the Huai River. Founded by Cai Shu Du, a younger brother of King Wu of Zhou, the state prospered through fertile agriculture and fortified trade settlements at Shangcai and Xincai. Occupying an exposed position on the northern frontier of Chu, Cai suffered repeated invasions, sieges and enforced relocations until Chu extinguished the state in 448 BC. \n\n Status: March; Capital: Shangcai; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Western Zhou to Warring States; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 448 BC; Succeeded by: State of Chu

name: State of Cao
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Cao was an ancient Chinese earldom established on the fertile North China Plain around modern Dingtao in south-western Shandong. Founded by Shu Zhenduo of Cao, a son of King Wen of Zhou, the state drew significant wealth from agricultural commerce and strategic riverine transport networks. However, diplomatic overreach and reckless military provocations against neighbouring Song during the Spring and Autumn period led directly to Cao's conquest and annexation in 487 BC. \n\n Status: Earldom; Capital: Dingtao; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Earl; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 487 BC; Succeeded by: State of Song

name: State of Chen
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Chen was a prominent Chinese feudal realm established in eastern Henan around its capital at Wanqiu in modern Huaiyang. Tracing royal descent from legendary Emperor Shun, its ruling house oversaw fourteen prosperous cities supported by intensive grain farming and silk weaving. Positioned between rival northern and southern superpowers, Chen frequently shifted allegiances during the Spring and Autumn period until King Hui of Chu annexed the territory and extinguished the ruling house. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Wanqiu; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion and ancestor worship; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 479 BC; Succeeded by: State of Chu

name: State of Cheng
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Cheng, historically identified with the early Zhou branch principality of Zheng, occupied strategic lands in central Henan near Xinzheng. Founded by members of the royal Ji clan, the state rose to premier geopolitical prominence during the early Eastern Zhou period by establishing an effective standing army and pioneering the first written legal code. Surrounded by aggressive Warring States rivals, the state defended its borders valiantly before being annexed by Han in 375 BC. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Xinzheng; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Western Zhou to Warring States; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: c. 408 BC; Succeeded by: State of Han

name: State of Chunyu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Chunyu was an ancient Chinese fiefdom established in central Shandong near modern Anqiu during the Western Zhou dynasty. Founded when King Wu enfeoffed Duke Chunyu, the minor state maintained modest agrarian settlements bordered by the neighbouring realms of Lai and Ji. Persistent military pressure and incursions from the migrating State of Qi fatally weakened the polity, prompting its ruler to flee abroad in 706 BC and precipitating its final dissolution. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Chunyu; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion and ancestor worship; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 706 BC; Succeeded by: State of Qi

name: State of Gao
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Gao was an ancient Chinese feudal fiefdom established on the North China Plain in western Shandong near modern Heze. Granted to an aristocratic lineage of the Zhou royal house following the overthrow of the Shang, the small polity administered local farming villages and preserved ancestral sacrificial rites. As royal Zhou authority decentralised across the early Spring and Autumn period, Gao was gradually absorbed by its larger and more assertive neighbouring states. \n\n Status: Feudal state; Capital: Gao; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: c. 800 BC; Succeeded by: State of Lu

name: State of Guo
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: Eastern Guo was an ancient Chinese vassal state established in central Henan at Zhidi near modern Xingyang during the Western Zhou dynasty. Founded by an uncle of King Wu of Zhou to guard the eastern approaches of the Central Plain, the state maintained vital military outposts along the Yellow River corridor. The principality preserved its local autonomy into the early Spring and Autumn period before being attacked, defeated and annexed by the State of Zheng in 767 BC. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Eastern Guo; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion and ancestor worship; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 767 BC; Succeeded by: State of Zheng

name: State of Guo
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: Western Guo was an important Chinese vassal duchy originally established at Yong in Shaanxi to guard the western frontiers of the Western Zhou royal domain. Forced eastward by recurring Quanrong tribal invasions, the state re-established its capital at Shangyang in the Sanmenxia gorge along the Yellow River. Celebrated for elite bronze casting and military leadership within the royal court, Western Guo was eventually conquered in 687 BC by Duke Xian of Jin through a famous stratagem. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Sanmenxia; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 687 BC; Succeeded by: State of Jin

name: State of Ji
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Ji was an ancient Chinese vassal principality established in northern Henan near modern Changyuan, later relocating to modern Zhengzhou. Founded by a son of the Duke of Zhou bearing the royal Ji surname, the realm furnished high-ranking ministers who advised the Zhou monarchs during the Western Zhou era. As neighbouring regional powers expanded during the early Spring and Autumn period, the state was overwhelmed and ultimately annexed into the territory of Zheng. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Zhengzhou; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: c. 750 BC; Succeeded by: State of Zheng

name: State of Ju
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Ju was an ancient Dongyi principality established in south-eastern Shandong around modern Ju County. Ruled by the noble Ji clan, the state constructed formidable city walls, preserved unique Eastern barbarian cultural customs and developed profitable iron casting and agriculture. Although fiercely defending its sovereignty against repeated assaults from Chu and Lu, internal political rivalries weakened the state, leading to its conquest and absorption by Qi in 431 BC. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Ju State; Common languages: Old Chinese and Dongyi dialects; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Western Zhou to Warring States; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 431 BC; Succeeded by: State of Qi

name: State of Qi
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Qi was a major Chinese power established in northern Shandong, governed from its sprawling walled capital at Linzi. Enfeoffed originally to the master strategist Jiang Ziya, Qi grew into a premier maritime and commercial empire through salt production, silk textiles and fisheries. Under Duke Huan and his chancellor Guan Zhong, Qi attained the first recognised Hegemon status among the feudal states, enduring until its conquest by Qin unified China in 221 BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Linzi; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Currency: Knife money; Historical era: Western Zhou to Warring States; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 221 BC; Succeeded by: Qin dynasty

name: State of Shao
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Shao was an internal Chinese fiefdom established in Shaanxi near modern Qishan, situated directly within the Western Zhou royal domain. Founded by the Duke of Shao, a trusted brother and advisor of King Wu, the state managed royal administrative affairs and commanded court ritual ceremonies. Shao officials continued serving as principal counsellors to the Zhou kings through the Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn periods until the state dissolved in 513 BC. \n\n Status: Fiefdom; Capital: Qishan; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 513 BC; Succeeded by: Eastern Zhou

name: State of Teng
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Teng was a minor Chinese viscounty established in southern Shandong around modern Tengzhou during the Western Zhou period. Founded by Shu Xiu of Cuo, a younger brother of King Wu of Zhou, the state maintained close diplomatic and cultural ties with neighbouring Lu. Renowned in classical philosophy as the birthplace of Mozi and architect Lu Ban, Teng retained its fragile autonomy through shifting alliances until King Kang of Song annexed it in 297 BC. \n\n Status: Viscounty; Capital: Tengzhou; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion and ancestor worship; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Viscount; Historical era: Western Zhou to Warring States; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 297 BC; Succeeded by: State of Song

name: State of Wen
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Wen was an ancient Chinese fiefdom established in northern Henan around modern Wenxian within the Western Zhou royal domain. Enfeoffed to royal judge Su Fensheng in recognition of his service during the conquest of Shang, the rulers served as chief judicial ministers at the Zhou court. Following regional rebellions and a refusal to aid the state against invading Di tribes, Wen was overrun and destroyed by northern nomadic forces in 650 BC. \n\n Status: Fiefdom; Capital: Wenxian; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship and Chinese folk religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Viscount; Historical era: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn; Established: c. 1043 BC; Disestablished: 650 BC; Succeeded by: State of Jin

name: State of Xu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Xu was an ancient Chinese feudal domain established in central Henan during the early Western Zhou period. Ruled by the Jiang lineage with the hereditary rank of baron, the polity occupied agricultural lands around modern Xuchang and maintained delicate relations with neighbouring vassals. The realm survived the collapse of Western Zhou royal authority before falling to the expanding southern power of Chu in 375 BC. \n\n Status: Feudal state; Capital: Xuchang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Baron; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Succeeded by: Chu

name: State of Yan
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Yan was an early Western Zhou principality located in the central plains of Henan near modern Yanling. Enfeoffed during the initial territorial settlements of the dynasty, this modest realm guarded local river corridors and agricultural settlements south of the Yellow River. The polity operated autonomously through the late second millennium BC before being eclipsed and absorbed by larger rival fiefdoms during the early Spring and Autumn period. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Yan; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Western Zhou; Historical region: Central Plains

name: State of Yan
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Yan was a major northern Chinese kingdom founded during the eleventh century BC by the Duke of Shao. Centred upon its fortified capital of Ji near modern Beijing, the realm defended the northern frontier of the Zhou world against nomadic steppe incursions through extensive earthen ramparts. It grew into one of the Seven Warring States, projecting influence from the Yellow River across the Liaodong Peninsula until conquered by Qin armies in 222 BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Ji; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Warring States period; Succeeded by: Qin dynasty; Currency: Knife money

name: State of Yuan
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Yuan was a minor aristocratic fief situated north of the Yellow River in present-day Jiyuan, Henan. Founded for a younger brother of King Wu of Zhou, the earldom belonged to the ruling Ji clan and exercised local authority throughout the Western Zhou era. During the Spring and Autumn period, Duke Wen of Jin laid siege to the city in 635 BC, earning its peaceful submission through steadfast adherence to a ten-day truce. \n\n Status: Earldom; Capital: Yuan; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Earl; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Succeeded by: Jin

name: State of Zhu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Zhu was an ancient Chinese fiefdom established in western Shandong near modern Changqing during the eleventh century BC. Governed by aristocrats claiming descent from the legendary Emperor Yao, the principality served as an eastern outpost of Zhou political influence. It retained its local independence through the early Spring and Autumn period before succumbing to regional neighbours as major states expanded across the Shandong peninsula. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Zhu; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Western Zhou; Historical region: Shandong

name: State of Zhu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Zhu was a small regional polity situated around modern Feicheng in western Shandong, traditionally traced to descendants of the Yellow Emperor bearing the Ren surname. The domain preserved ancient ritual traditions and bronze metalworking, intermarrying with prominent noble families of the neighbouring State of Lu. It maintained an autonomous posture during the early centuries of the Eastern Zhou period until being absorbed by the State of Qi. \n\n Status: Regional state; Capital: Zhu; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Succeeded by: Qi; Historical region: Central Plains

name: State of Zou
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Zou, originally known as Zhulou or Zhu, was an ancient Chinese principality situated in southern Shandong. Governed by the Cao lineage with the rank of viscount, the realm frequently clashed with its larger neighbour Lu while developing a sophisticated scholarly and ritual tradition. Despite enduring for over six centuries, the state was ultimately annexed by the southern kingdom of Chu during the Warring States period. \n\n Status: Viscounty; Capital: Zou; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Viscount; Historical era: Warring States period; Succeeded by: Chu

name: Three Guards
description: The Three Guards was a short-lived administrative collective formed in eastern China following the Zhou conquest of the Shang dynasty. King Wu of Zhou appointed his three younger brothers to oversee the conquered Shang heartland from Chaoge alongside the puppet prince Wu Geng. Following King Wu's death, the three princes allied with Shang loyalists and regional tribes in open rebellion against the Duke of Zhou's regency, triggering a three-year military campaign that crushed the uprising. \n\n Status: Royal military domain; Capital: Chaoge; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Shang folk religion; Government: Feudal collective; Historical era: Western Zhou; Disestablished: 1041 BC; Succeeded by: Wey

name: State of Wei
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Wei, commonly styled Wey to distinguish it from its larger namesake, was a prominent Zhou dynasty duchy situated in northern Henan. Founded for Kangshu of Feng by the Duke of Zhou, the realm was renowned for its skilled artisans, poetry and strategic position along the Yellow River plain. Though severely weakened by Di nomad invasions in the seventh century BC, the resilient polity survived as a minor protectorate down to the late Qin dynasty. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Zhaoge; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 209 BC

name: Kingdom of Israel
description: The Kingdom of Israel, traditionally remembered as the United Monarchy, was an ancient Israelite realm spanning Cisjordan and parts of Transjordan in the Southern Levant. Emerging from a confederation of twelve Hebrew tribes under Saul, the kingdom established its royal seat at Jerusalem under David and Solomon, who constructed monumental fortifications and the first central temple. Following Solomon's death around 930 BC, tribal grievances over taxation and royal authority fractured the realm into northern Israel and southern Judah. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Jerusalem; Common languages: Early Hebrew; Religion: Yahwism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Preceded by: Twelve Tribes of Israel; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Israel and Kingdom of Judah

name: State of Yang
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Yang was a minor Zhou principality located along the Fen River valley in present-day Hongdong, Shanxi. Created for members of the royal Ji clan during the consolidation of the Western Zhou dynasty, the realm guarded inland agricultural valleys and local transport routes. Its strategic proximity to the rising power of Jin proved fatal, leading to its conquest and annexation by Duke Xian of Jin during the seventh century BC. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Yang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Succeeded by: Jin; Historical region: Shanxi

name: State of Chu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Chu was an expansive southern Chinese kingdom that developed along the middle reaches of the Yangtze and Han river valleys. Governed by the Mi and Xiong dynasties, the polity adopted a distinct culture blending northern Zhou court ritual with indigenous southern traditions, expanding into a formidable imperial contender. Its rulers were among the first to cast aside the Zhou royal titles in favour of declaring themselves kings, dominating central and southern China until conquered by Qin in 223 BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Danyang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Warring States period; Succeeded by: Qin dynasty; Currency: Ancient Chinese coinage

name: State of Jiang
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Jiang was a small Chinese vassal principality established in southern Henan near modern Gushi during the early Western Zhou dynasty. Enfeoffed to Bo Ling, a son of the Duke of Zhou, the realm served as an aristocratic march securing southern borderlands. The state maintained its ancestral rites through several centuries until the aggressive northward expansion of the Kingdom of Chu brought about its final annexation in 617 BC. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Jiang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ji; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 617 BC; Succeeded by: Chu

name: State of Jin
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Jin was one of the preeminent regional powers of ancient China, dominating the fertile basins of modern Shanxi from the Western Zhou into the Warring States period. Founded for Shuyu of Tang, the marquisate rose to become the leading hegemon of the Central Plains, frequently marshalling allied armies against Chu. Severe aristocratic competition eventually destabilised the ducal house, culminating in the historic three-way partition between the ministerial families of Han, Zhao and Wei. \n\n Status: Marquisate; Capital: Houma; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor veneration and folk religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Succeeded by: Han, Zhao and Wei; Currency: Spade money

name: State of Lu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Lu was a deeply influential Chinese principality situated in southwestern Shandong, founded during the eleventh century BC for Boqin, the eldest son of the Duke of Zhou. Renowned for its meticulous preservation of traditional Zhou rites, governance customs and literary heritage, the capital of Qufu emerged as a preeminent centre of classical learning and the birthplace of Confucius. Despite its enduring moral prestige, Lu suffered territorial encroachment from neighbouring states before Chu annexed it in 256 BC. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Qufu; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor veneration and folk religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 256 BC; Succeeded by: Chu

name: State of Mao
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Mao was a minor Zhou dynasty fief located near modern Jinxiang and Juye in southwestern Shandong. Founded for Mao Shu, the third son of the Duke of Zhou, the polity enjoyed close diplomatic and family ties with the neighbouring senior branch ruling the State of Lu. It managed to preserve its communal autonomy until the mid-Spring and Autumn period, when an escalating border dispute prompted the Duke of Zou to invade and extinguish the realm. \n\n Status: Feudal state; Capital: Mao State; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ji; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Historical region: Shandong; Succeeded by: Zou

name: State of Shen
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Shen was an ancient Chinese earldom ruled by the Jiang lineage, situated in southern Henan near modern Nanyang and Shenqiu. Established during the Western Zhou dynasty to anchor royal influence across the Han River corridor, the state acted as a pivotal march against southern tribal confederacies. In the early seventh century BC, King Wen of Chu launched a sustained campaign northward, subjugating Shen and transforming its territory into a frontier county of Chu. \n\n Status: Earldom; Capital: Shenqiu; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Jiang; Ruler title: Earl; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Succeeded by: Chu

name: State of Song
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Song was an important ancient Chinese domain established in eastern Henan following the Zhou conquest, created to maintain the ancestral sacrifices of the fallen Shang dynasty royal line. Governed from Shangqiu by descendants of the Shang kings, the wealthy duchy prospered through extensive regional commerce and fertile agricultural plains. Although renowned for its ritual observance and commercial prominence, Song was partitioned and annexed by an alliance of Qi, Chu and Wei in 286 BC. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Shangqiu; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor veneration and folk religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Warring States period; Disestablished: 286 BC; Succeeded by: Qi

name: State of Xiaozhu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Xiaozhu, also known as Lesser Zhu or Ni, was an ancient Chinese principality situated around modern Zaozhuang in southern Shandong. Originating as a cadet offshoot of the neighbouring State of Zou, the small domain retained autonomy under the Cao lineage throughout the turbulent political shifts of the Eastern Zhou era. It survived until the mid-fourth century BC, when Chu's northern military expansion ultimately absorbed the territory. \n\n Status: Regional state; Capital: Xiaozhu; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Warring States period; Disestablished: 335 BC; Succeeded by: Chu; Historical region: Shandong

name: State of Xing
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Xing was a northern Chinese marquisate founded by the Zhou royal house on the eastern plains of modern Hebei near Xingtai. Ruled by the Ji lineage, the state functioned as a crucial strategic bastion shielding the agricultural heartland of the Central Plains against nomadic incursions from the Di peoples. Severe barbarian incursions in the seventh century BC forced the relocation of its court, leaving the weakened domain vulnerable to partition between Jin and Wey in 632 BC. \n\n Status: Marquisate; Capital: Xingtai; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 632 BC; Succeeded by: Jin and Wey

name: State of Ying
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Ying was a regional Chinese principality located around modern Pingdingshan and Lushan in central Henan. Enfeoffed to a son of King Cheng of Zhou, the domain prospered as a centre of bronze metallurgical craftsmanship and southern frontier diplomacy. Ying successfully defended its sovereignty through the Western Zhou period before succumbing to political pressure and final military annexation by the State of Chu in 646 BC. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Ying; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor veneration and folk religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ji; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 646 BC; Succeeded by: Chu

name: Atun
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Atun, also known as Tunna or Tynna, was a Luwian Neo-Hittite kingdom situated in southern Cappadocia at the northern foot of the Taurus Mountains near the Cilician Gates. Flourishing during the early Iron Age from its fortified centre near modern Niğde, the state controlled vital mineral extraction sites and strategic mountain trade corridors. It maintained regional autonomy alongside neighbouring Tabal until coming under tribute and eventual incorporation into the Neo-Assyrian Empire in the late eighth century BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Tyana; Common languages: Luwian; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Anatolia

name: Bit Khalupi
label: aramean polities
description: Bit Khalupi was an ancient Aramean kingdom established around the confluence of the Khabur and Euphrates rivers in eastern Syria. Governed from the fortified city of Suru, the realm served as an important hub for riverine commerce and pastoral migration across Upper Mesopotamia. In 883 BC, local factions joined an armed uprising against Neo-Assyrian authority, prompting King Ashurnasirpal II to execute a ruthless punitive campaign that permanently annexed the principality. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Suru; Common languages: Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 883 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Upper Mesopotamia

name: Chaironeia
label: greek poleis
description: Chaironeia was an ancient Greek polis located in western Boeotia along the strategic route traversing the Cephissus river valley. Positioned beneath Mount Thourion northwest of Thebes, the settlement defended fertile agricultural plains and controlled access between central Greece and the northern passes. While asserting civic independence during the Archaic and Classical eras, the city frequently navigated Boeotian confederate politics before achieving wider historical fame as the setting of decisive Hellenistic military clashes. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Chaeronea; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Classical Antiquity; Historical region: Boeotia

name: Drangians
description: The Drangians were an ancient eastern Iranian tribal confederation established in the endorheic Sistan basin across the modern borderlands of Iran and Afghanistan. Settled around the wetlands of Lake Hamun and the lower Helmand River, the population developed sophisticated irrigation networks and pastoral traditions tailored to the arid environment. Their autonomous tribal structures formed the institutional basis for the later satrapy of Drangiana following absorption into the Median and Achaemenid imperial realms. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Iranian; Religion: Iranian polytheism; Government: Tribal council of chieftains; Historical era: Iron Age; Historical region: Sistan; Succeeded by: Median Empire

name: Gozo
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (outside phoenicia)
description: Gozo, known in antiquity as Gaulos, was an autonomous Phoenician island city-state in the central Mediterranean situated northwest of Malta. Capitalising on natural harbours and fertile rolling hills, the colony served as an essential maritime revictualling point and trading outpost along trans-Mediterranean shipping lanes. The settlement preserved independent civic self-governance and Levantine religious rituals through the early first millennium BC until gradually coming under Carthaginian hegemony. \n\n Status: Island city-state; Capital: Victoria Gozo; Common languages: Phoenician; Religion: Phoenician polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Carthaginian Empire; Historical region: Mediterranean

name: Hilakku
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Hilakku was a prominent Luwian Neo-Hittite kingdom situated in the rugged highlands of Cilicia Trachea along the Taurus Mountains of southeastern Anatolia. Descended from Bronze Age political traditions, the mountaineers maintained a formidable martial reputation and controlled strategic mountain passes linking central Anatolia to the Mediterranean coast. Hilakku repeatedly repelled and resisted Neo-Assyrian military incursions before ultimately submitting to imperial authority in the late eighth century BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Silifke; Common languages: Luwian; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Preceded by: Tarhuntassa; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Immerinu
label: aramean polities
description: Immerinu was a small Aramean principality that emerged along the upper Euphrates valley near Harran around the turn of the first millennium BC. Mentioned in contemporary Neo-Assyrian administrative tablets and royal inscriptions, the realm drew wealth from regional riverine trade and agricultural livestock. It preserved sovereign autonomy under local rulers such as King Ger-Hadad before being subordinated as an Assyrian tributary during the campaigns of Shalmaneser III. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Immerinu; Common languages: Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Upper Mesopotamia

name: Izalla
label: aramean polities
description: Izalla, also recorded as Bit Yahiri, was an ancient Aramean kingdom situated in the rugged plateau of Tur Abdin and the Tektek mountains of upper Mesopotamia. Renowned throughout antiquity for its high-quality wine production and highland defensibility, the state acted as a key buffer between the Syrian plains and the northern mountains. Following an extended period of independence, Izalla was reduced to tributary status by King Adad-nirari II of Assyria in 891 BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Mardin; Common languages: Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 891 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Upper Mesopotamia

name: Jushi Kingdom
label: tarim basin
description: The Jushi Kingdom was an ancient oasis state established in the Turpan Basin of the eastern Tian Shan by pastoral and agricultural communities linked with the Subeshi culture. Centred upon the remarkable cliff-top walled city of Jiaohe, the kingdom prospered from viticulture and its vital position along the northern trans-Eurasian trade routes. The polity maintained full sovereignty until Chinese military expeditions under General Zhao Ponu forced it into clientage to the Han dynasty in 108 BC. \n\n Status: Oasis kingdom; Capital: Jiaohe; Common languages: Tocharian; Religion: Steppe polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical Antiquity; Succeeded by: Han dynasty; Historical region: Tarim Basin

name: Katak
label: aramean polities
description: Katak was an ancient Aramean and Luwian state located in northern Syria and the adjacent borders of southeastern Anatolia. Emerged in the aftermath of Bronze Age imperial collapses, the principality forged strategic diplomatic alliances with Arpad and neighbouring Syro-Hittite polities to resist Mesopotamian expansion. Its independent political existence ended during the westward campaigns of Tiglath-Pileser III, which shattered local coalitions and annexed the territory into the Neo-Assyrian Empire around 740 BC. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Katak; Common languages: Aramaic and Luwian; Religion: Levantine polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 740 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Northern Syria

name: Khindanu
label: aramean polities
description: Khindanu was an Aramean riverine state that flourished along the middle Euphrates south of the Khabur confluence during the early first millennium BC. Drawing economic prosperity from control of trans-desert caravan traffic and river navigation, the kingdom maintained independent governance under local dynasts. name: Kingdom of Ammon
description: The Kingdom of Ammon was an ancient Semitic polity situated east of the Jordan River in the fertile highlands between the Jabbok and Arnon valleys. Centred on the fortified royal stronghold of Rabbath Ammon, the nation worshipped the national god Milcom and maintained an active role in regional trade networks spanning the Arabian desert and the Levant. The kingdom vigorously defended its sovereignty against neighbouring Israelite, Moabite and Aramean rivals until becoming a vassal of regional empires. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Rabbath Ammon; Common languages: Ammonite; Religion: Canaanite polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Historical region: Transjordan; Succeeded by: Neo-Babylonian Empire

name: Kingdom of Urartu
description: The Kingdom of Urartu was a powerful Iron Age highland state that arose around Lake Van across the mountainous Armenian Highlands. Drawing strength from formidable cyclopean stone citadels, advanced metallurgy and sophisticated hydraulic engineering, the Urartian monarchs unified local Nairi tribes into an expansive confederation. Under kings such as Arame and Sarduri I, the kingdom successfully challenged the hegemony of the Neo-Assyrian Empire across eastern Anatolia and the northern Zagros. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Sugunia; Common languages: Urartian and Akkadian; Religion: Urartian polytheism; Government: Hereditary absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Preceded by: Nairi; Succeeded by: Median Empire

name: Laqi
label: aramean polities
description: Laqi was an Aramean tribal principality established on both banks of the middle Euphrates between the Khabur and Balikh river systems. Exploiting key river crossings and desert caravan corridors, the confederation exercised autonomous control over pastoralist clans and fortified trading settlements. The expansion of the Neo-Assyrian state under Adad-nirari II terminated its independence around 895 BC, and subsequent regional rebellions were crushed with devastating force by King Ashurnasirpal II. \n\n Status: Tribal principality; Capital: Laqi; Common languages: Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Confederation of chieftains; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 895 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Upper Mesopotamia

name: Maleth

description: Maleth was an autonomous Phoenician maritime settlement and island polity founded on Malta during the early tenth century BC. Situated centrally in the Mediterranean, its natural harbours offered exceptional shelter and replenishment for merchant vessels navigating between the Levant, Sicily and the western Mediterranean. The colony fostered distinctive craft industries and Phoenician cultural traditions, exercising local autonomy for several centuries prior to being integrated into the Carthaginian maritime sphere. \n\n Status: Island colony; Capital: Valletta; Common languages: Phoenician; Religion: Phoenician polytheism; Government: Merchant oligarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Carthaginian Empire; Historical region: Central Mediterranean

name: Mamblu
label: aramean polities
description: Mamblu was an Aramean city-state situated in upper Mesopotamia near modern Sultantepe north of Harran. The polity centred around the settlement of Khurizina, where ancient administrative archives and a noted cuneiform library have been identified. Maintaining autonomous communal institutions while engaging in diplomatic exchange with the burgeoning Assyrian kingdom, the realm gradually faded from historical records after being incorporated into the imperial provincial network in the ninth century BC. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Mamblu; Common languages: Aramaic and Akkadian; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Upper Mesopotamia

name: Nasibin
label: aramean polities
description: Nasibin was an ancient Aramean principality situated at the southern foot of the Tur Abdin plateau on the banks of the Jaghjagh River. Recorded in contemporary records as Naṣibīna, the fortified town occupied an indispensable node along east-west trade arteries connecting the upper Tigris with the Syrian plains. It defended its sovereignty through the tenth century BC before falling into the expanding territorial orbit of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Nusaybin; Common languages: Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Upper Mesopotamia

name: Pattin
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Pattin, also recorded in ancient inscriptions as Unqi or Patina, was an influential Luwian Neo-Hittite state centred in the fertile Amuq plain of northern Syria. Governed from the fortified city of Kunulua, the kingdom controlled vital access routes between the Cilician coast, the Orontes valley and inland Syria. It resisted Mesopotamian imperial pressures through diplomatic coalitions until King Tiglath-Pileser III captured its capital in 738 BC, reorganising the realm into an Assyrian province. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Kunulua; Common languages: Luwian and Aramaic; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 738 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Shinukta
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Shinukta was a small Neo-Hittite principality located in southern Cappadocia near the headwaters of the Zamanti and Seyhan rivers. Bordering the larger realms of Atun and Tabal, the polity controlled highland agricultural pastures and mineral wealth along the northern approaches to Cilicia. Though initially tributary to the Neo-Assyrian Empire under local dynasts like King Kiakku, a refusal to deliver tribute in 718 BC led to Sargon II destroying the capital and annexing its territory. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Niğde; Common languages: Luwian; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 718 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Anatolia

name: Shugab
label: aramean polities
description: Shugab was a short-lived Aramean riverine state established along the upper Euphrates between Birecik and Samosata during the tenth century BC. Bordered by Bit Adini to the south and Kummukh to the north, the principality controlled valuable ferry crossings and irrigated terrace farming. The realm preserved complete political autonomy throughout the tenth century BC before capitulating to the westward military campaigns of Shalmaneser III and passing under direct Assyrian control. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Birecik; Common languages: Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Upper Mesopotamia

name: Shuhi
label: aramean polities
description: Shuhi was an ancient Aramean-influenced principality situated along the middle Euphrates near modern Anah in western Iraq. Inheriting administrative and cultural customs from ancient Babylonia, the kingdom maintained commercial ties with the Mesopotamian heartland while defending its autonomy against steppe nomads. The polity was compelled to accept tributary obligations to Assyria around 895 BC, and a subsequent regional uprising brought devastating reprisal from Ashurnasirpal II. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Anah; Common languages: Aramaic and Akkadian; Religion: Mesopotamian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Middle Euphrates

name: State of Han

description: The State of Han was an early Chinese feudal domain established in the Wei and Yellow River valleys across modern Shaanxi and Shanxi during the Western Zhou period. Created for a son of King Wu of Zhou with the rank of marquis, the realm secured strategic river crossings and defended the central plains against western border peoples. The state maintained its sovereign standing until being annexed by the rising power of Jin during the eighth century BC. \n\n Status: Marquisate; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ji; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Western Zhou; Succeeded by: Jin

name: State of Huo
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Huo was an ancient Chinese principality situated around modern Huozhou in Shanxi. Established during the Western Zhou period for Shu Chu of Huo, a younger brother of King Wu, the realm acted as a strategic bastion guarding the inland Fen River corridor. The domain retained its ancestral governance into the Spring and Autumn period until Duke Xian of Jin invaded and conquered the territory in 661 BC. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Huo State; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ji; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Succeeded by: Jin

name: State of Ji
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Ji was an ancient Chinese city-state located on the northern plains near modern Beijing. Tracing its founding to the Shang and early Western Zhou eras, the settlement was governed by aristocrats traditionally identified as descendants of the legendary Emperor Yao. Centred upon the fortified stronghold of Jicheng, the small polity defended its autonomy until being conquered and absorbed by the expanding State of Yan during the seventh century BC. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Beijing; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 700 BC; Succeeded by: Yan

name: State of Luo
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Luo was a minor Chinese feudal polity located along the Han and Yangtze river systems in modern Henan and Hubei. Sharing ancestral ties with the ruling lineage of Chu, the realm developed distinct cultural customs while maintaining its independence through the Western Zhou dynasty. The state was eventually attacked and dismantled by King Wu of Chu in 690 BC, its population being forcibly relocated southward toward the Miluo River. \n\n Status: Feudal state; Capital: Miluo; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 690 BC; Succeeded by: Chu

name: State of Zhang
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Zhang was an ancient Chinese principality situated in western Shandong near modern Dongping. Established for a cadet branch descended from the renowned statesman Jiang Ziya, the realm belonged to the Jiang clan and initially exercised local autonomy under the Western Zhou court. By the Spring and Autumn period, it had become a client of the State of Ji before Duke Huan of Qi annexed the domain in 664 BC. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Zhang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Jiang; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 664 BC; Succeeded by: Qi

name: Surug
label: aramean polities
description: Surug was an Aramean riverine state established along the upper Euphrates between Harran and Carchemish around the turn of the first millennium BC. Centred upon the ancient settlement of modern Suruç, the polity profited from flourishing trade across Upper Mesopotamia and sustained an autonomous tribal monarchy under rulers like King Gaidu. It preserved its sovereignty throughout the tenth century BC before falling into the tributary orbit of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. \n\n Status: Riverine state; Capital: Suruç; Common languages: Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Upper Mesopotamia

name: Takalik Abaj
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Takalik Abaj was a major Mesoamerican ceremonial and commercial centre situated along the fertile Pacific coastal slope of modern Guatemala. Beginning in the early first millennium BC, the city-state flourished as a vital hub of regional exchange, linking highland and lowland trade networks through the trade of cacao, obsidian and jade. Its monumental stone architecture and sculptures uniquely bridged Olmec stylistic traditions with the emergence of early Maya civilisation. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Takalik Abaj; Common languages: Mixe-Zoquean and Mayan; Religion: Mesoamerican polytheism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Historical era: Preclassic Maya; Historical region: Mesoamerica

name: Til-Abni
label: aramean polities
description: Til-Abni was an ancient Aramean principality situated in upper Mesopotamia between Harran and Bit Zamani. Drawing strength from fortified settlements across the northern Euphrates basin, the state preserved its independence under local leaders such as Prince Khabin. Its resistance against Assyrian territorial expansion ended in 877 BC when King Ashurnasirpal II conducted a devastating campaign across the region, compelling the submission of Til-Abni and its neighbours. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Til-Abni; Common languages: Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 877 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Torone
label: greek poleis
description: Torone was an ancient Greek maritime polis located on the southwest tip of the Sithonia peninsula in Chalkidike. Endowed with a sheltered and spacious natural harbour, the city thrived through maritime commerce, fishing and timber exports across the northern Aegean. The community governed its own civic affairs autonomously from the early Iron Age until the Persian expansion across Thrace and Macedonia temporarily compromised its independence in 481 BC. \n\n Status: Maritime polis; Capital: Torone; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Archaic Greece; Historical region: Chalkidike

name: Tuwanuwa
description: Tuwanuwa was an ancient Luwian Neo-Hittite kingdom situated in southern Cappadocia around the modern town of Kemerhisar. Occupying an essential strategic position north of the Cilician Gates, the realm controlled vital overland transit routes and mineral resources of the central Taurus mountains. Under local rulers such as King Warpalawas, the state commissioned monumental rock reliefs and preserved its sovereignty before being incorporated into the Neo-Assyrian Empire. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Tuwanuwa; Common languages: Luwian; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Cappadocia

name: Kingdom of Dʿmt
description: The Kingdom of Dʿmt was an ancient Ethio-Sabaean realm established across the highlands of Eritrea and northern Ethiopia. Governed from the ceremonial capital of Yeha, the kingdom engaged in extensive trans-Red Sea commerce and constructed monumental dry-stone temples exhibiting South Arabian architectural influences. The polity flourished from the late tenth century BC until its decentralisation into smaller local polities that subsequently contributed to the rise of the Aksumite Empire. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Yeha; Common languages: Ethio-Sabaic; Religion: South Arabian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mukarrib; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Aksum; Historical region: Horn of Africa

name: Gurgum
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Gurgum was a Luwian Neo-Hittite kingdom that occupied the valleys around the modern city of Kahramanmaraş in southeastern Anatolia. Centred upon its fortified capital of Marqas, the state prospered from highland agriculture and strategic passes through the Taurus Mountains. The kingdom maintained an independent dynastic line that produced numerous hieroglyphic Luwian royal monuments until Sargon II overthrew its last monarch in 711 BC, annexing the realm into the Neo-Assyrian Empire. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Marqas; Common languages: Hieroglyphic Luwian; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 711 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Raqamatu
label: aramean polities
description: Raqamatu was an ancient Aramean kingdom situated along the upper reaches of the Khabur River in northern Mesopotamia. Formerly known under Assyrian administration as Gidara, the fortified city was seized by Temanite Arameans during the late tenth century BC and developed into an independent local bastion. The realm endured until King Adad-nirari II of Assyria launched a successful siege in 898 BC, deporting its ruler Muquru and annexing the territory. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Raqamatu; Common languages: Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 898 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Upper Mesopotamia

name: Kingdom of Israel
description: The Kingdom of Israel, commonly known as the Northern Kingdom, was an ancient Israelite state established in the central and northern Southern Levant following the secession of ten tribes from the United Monarchy. Ruled from its fortified hilltop capital at Samaria by successive dynasties such as the Omrides and Nimshides, the kingdom controlled fertile tracts across Galilee and Gilead. It remained a formidable regional military and commercial power until falling to the Neo-Assyrian Empire in 722 BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Samaria; Common languages: Biblical Hebrew; Religion: Yahwism and Canaanite polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Preceded by: United Monarchy of Israel; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Kingdom of Judah
description: The Kingdom of Judah was an ancient Israelite realm centred in the rugged highlands south of Jerusalem, bordered by the Dead Sea and the coastal plain. Governed uninterruptedly by descendants of the Davidic dynasty following the fracture of the United Monarchy, the kingdom maintained its religious and political life around the Temple of Jerusalem. Judah preserved its sovereign autonomy through shifting Levantine coalitions until becoming an Assyrian tributary state in the late eighth century BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Jerusalem; Common languages: Biblical Hebrew; Religion: Yahwism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of David; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Preceded by: United Monarchy of Israel

name: Bit Agusi
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Bit Agusi was an influential Aramean state in the northern Levant established in the early ninth century BC by Gusi of Yakhan. Governing extensive territories between Azaz and Aleppo from its formidable capital at Arpad, the kingdom directed diplomatic coalitions against Assyrian territorial encroachments. After enduring a bitter three-year siege, Arpad fell to the armies of King Tiglath-Pileser III in 740 BC, terminating the kingdom's sovereignty and incorporating it into an Assyrian province. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Arpad; Common languages: Aramaic; Religion: Ancient Semitic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 740 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Ellipi
description: Ellipi was an ancient highland kingdom situated in the western Zagros mountains across modern Luristan and Kermanshah in Iran. Sharing strong linguistic and cultural affinities with neighbouring Elam, the realm controlled strategic transit valleys linking the Mesopotamian plain with the Iranian plateau. Under kings like Dalta, Ellipi skilfully balanced relations with Assyria and Elam until dynastic disputes following his death invited destructive foreign military intervention. \n\n Status: Highland kingdom; Capital: Ellipi; Common languages: Elamite and Iranian dialects; Religion: Elamite polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Median Empire; Historical region: Zagros

name: Hadrumetum
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (outside phoenicia)
description: Hadrumetum was an autonomous Phoenician maritime colony founded on the Gulf of Hammamet in modern Tunisia during the ninth century BC. Predating the foundation of neighbouring Carthage, the settlement grew into an essential port of call and export centre for north African olive oil and grain. The city maintained civic self-government under its own merchant elite until Carthage established political hegemony across the eastern Maghreb during the sixth century BC. \n\n Status: Island city-state; Capital: Hadrumetum; Common languages: Phoenician; Religion: Phoenician polytheism; Government: Merchant oligarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Carthaginian Empire; Historical region: North Africa

name: Hippo Regius
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (outside phoenicia)
description: Hippo Regius was an early Phoenician coastal colony and maritime trading hub established on the Numidian shore in modern Annaba, northeastern Algeria. Boasting a protected harbour sheltered by Cape Rosa, the city flourished as an emporium facilitating maritime commerce between the Levant, the Tyrrhenian Sea and indigenous Berber tribes. It preserved civic independence through centuries of Mediterranean trade before passing under Carthaginian and later Numidian royal control. \n\n Status: Coastal city-state; Capital: Annaba; Common languages: Phoenician and Berber; Religion: Phoenician polytheism; Government: Merchant oligarchy; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Carthaginian Empire; Historical region: North Africa

name: Kingdom of the Mannai
description: The Kingdom of the Mannai was an ancient Iron Age state situated in northwestern Iran south and southeast of Lake Urmia. Centred upon the fortified stronghold of Izirtu near modern Saqqez, the Mannaeans developed an advanced urban civilisation known for monumental defensive architecture and skilled horse breeding. The kingdom pursued flexible diplomatic alliances between Urartu and Assyria to safeguard its independence, flourishing until its subjugation and incorporation into the Median Empire. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Izirtu; Common languages: Mannaean; Religion: Ancient Near Eastern polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Median Empire; Historical region: Iranian Plateau

name: Kummuh
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Kummuh was a Luwian Neo-Hittite kingdom situated on the western bank of the Upper Euphrates in southeastern Anatolia. Governed from the fortified river city of Samosata, the state derived significant wealth from its control over crucial river crossings and fertile agricultural terraces. The monarchy preserved cordial diplomatic and tributary relations with the Neo-Assyrian Empire for more than a century before Sargon II accused its king of conspiring with Urartu and annexed the territory in 708 BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Samosata; Common languages: Hieroglyphic Luwian; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Disestablished: 708 BC; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire

name: Myrina
label: greek poleis
description: Myrina was an ancient Greek city-state situated on the coast of Aeolis in western Anatolia, located near modern Aliağa in Turkey. Situated on an inlet at the mouth of the Pythikos River, the polis formed part of the Aeolian Dodecapolis and derived wealth from maritime trade, pottery manufacturing and olive cultivation. The city maintained its civic autonomy through the Archaic era before falling under the suzerainty of the Lydian kingdom and the Achaemenid Empire. \n\n Status: Maritime polis; Capital: Myrina; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Archaic Greece; Historical region: Aeolis

name: Panchala Kingdom
label: mahajanapadas
description: The Panchala Kingdom was an ancient Indo-Aryan realm situated in northern India across the fertile Ganges-Yamuna Doab around modern Rohilkhand. Divided administratively into northern Panchala with its capital at Ahichchhatra and southern Panchala centred at Kampilya, the state stood as a leading cultural and political power of the late Vedic period. Celebrated for patronage of Vedic philosophers and religious scholars, the kingdom later transformed into an oligarchic republic and ranked among the sixteen Mahajanapadas. \n\n Status: Mahajanapada; Capital: Ahichchhatra; Common languages: Vedic Sanskrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Nanda Empire; Historical region: Northern India

name: Quwê
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Quwê was a Luwian Neo-Hittite kingdom situated in the fertile coastal plain of Cilicia Pedias in southeastern Anatolia. Governed from Tarsus and Adana, the realm commanded overland transit corridors between Anatolia and Syria while dominating lucrative maritime trade along the northeastern Mediterranean. Quwê maintained its independence through local dynasts until successive military campaigns by Shalmaneser III and later Neo-Assyrian monarchs reduced it to an imperial province. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Tarsus; Common languages: Luwian and Phoenician; Religion: Luwian polytheism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Cilicia

name: State of Sui
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Sui, also identified in contemporary bronze epigraphy as Zeng, was an ancient Chinese principality situated along the strategic Suizao corridor in modern Hubei. Founded during the early Western Zhou to secure the northern approaches to the Central Plains against the expanding southern power of Chu, the realm was celebrated for extraordinary bronze casting, as demonstrated by the famous tomb of Marquis Yi. The state retained its autonomy as a regional military buffer until Chu annexed it in the fifth century BC. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Suizhou; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ji; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Succeeded by: Chu

name: Troizen
label: greek poleis
description: Troizen was an ancient Greek polis situated on the northeastern coast of the Argolid peninsula in the Peloponnese. Famed in Hellenic mythology as the birthplace of the hero Theseus, the city commanded fertile coastal lowlands facing the Saronic Gulf and fostered close cultural connections with Athens. The polis exercised civic autonomy through the Archaic and Classical periods, participating prominently in the Hellenic League during the Persian Wars. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Troizen; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Classical Antiquity; Historical region: Argolis

name: Videha Kingdom
description: The Videha Kingdom was an ancient realm of north-eastern South Asia situated across the eastern Gangetic plain and the foothills of modern Nepal. Centred upon its magnificent capital of Mithila, the state rose to prominence during the late Vedic period under philosopher-kings like Janaka, who hosted famous Upanishadic theological debates. The kingdom subsequently transitioned into an aristocratic republic and joined the powerful Vajjika League against Magadhan expansion. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Mithila; Common languages: Vedic Sanskrit; Religion: Historical Vedic religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Vajjika League; Historical region: Mithila

name: State of Qin
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Qin was an ancient Chinese principality founded in the western frontier valleys of modern Gansu and Shaanxi. Originating as horse breeders and border defenders for the Western Zhou royal court, Qin expanded eastward into the fertile Guanzhong basin by subduing the Rong tribes. Through profound administrative, legalist and military reforms orchestrated by Shang Yang, the kingdom transformed into an unstoppable military power that conquered all rival states to establish the Qin Empire in 221 BC. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Xianyang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Centralised legalist monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Warring States period; Succeeded by: Qin dynasty; Currency: Ban Liang coins

name: Luhuti
label: luwian-aramean polities;aramean polities
description: Luhuti, also attested in ancient inscriptions as Lu'ash, was a Neo-Hittite and Aramean realm situated in northern Syria between Aleppo and the Orontes valley. Centred upon the fortified stronghold of Hatarikka, the principality commanded productive agrarian plains and strategic overland trade routes. Luhuti formed the northern core of a united kingdom under King Zakkur of Hamath before falling victim to Neo-Assyrian military expansion in the eighth century BC. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Hatarikka; Common languages: Aramaic and Luwian; Religion: Levantine polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Historical region: Northern Syria

name: Parsua
description: Parsua was an ancient Iranian tribal kingdom located in the central western Zagros mountains across modern Kermanshah in Iran. Attested frequently in Neo-Assyrian royal inscriptions from the ninth century BC onward, the realm comprised a confederation of autonomous chieftains defending highland mountain valleys. The polity preserved its tribal structure and independence against intermittent Assyrian raids before becoming integrated into the wider Median realm. \n\n Status: Tribal kingdom; Capital: Parsua; Common languages: Old Iranian; Religion: Iranian polytheism; Government: Confederation of chieftains; Historical era: Iron Age; Succeeded by: Median Empire; Historical region: Zagros

name: Akraiphia
label: greek poleis
description: Akraiphia was an ancient Greek polis situated in eastern Boeotia on the steep slopes of Mount Ptoum near Lake Copais. The city derived widespread prestige from the adjacent sanctuary and oracle of Apollo Ptoios, which drew pilgrims and emissaries from across the Hellenic world. While frequently subject to Theban political influence, Akraiphia guarded its civic institutions and local independence during periods of Boeotian League dissolution. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Akraifnio; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Classical Antiquity; Historical region: Boeotia

name: Alalkomenai
label: greek poleis
description: Alalkomenai was a venerable ancient Greek polis situated at the foot of Mount Tilphossium in western Boeotia near Lake Copais. The town was celebrated throughout Hellas for its ancient sanctuary dedicated to Athena Alalkomeneis, where tradition held that the goddess herself had been nurtured. Because of its strictly sacred inviolable character, the polis maintained civic autonomy and enjoyed protection from military sack across numerous regional conflicts. \n\n Status: Sacred city-state; Capital: Alalcomenae; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Classical Antiquity; Historical region: Boeotia
